text:
# NASA Glenn Research Center - Combustion Science Program & Spacecraft Fire Safety Overview

Source: NASA Glenn Research Center Physical Sciences Program
URL: https://www.nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science/
Affiliated Facilities: Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Zero Gravity Research Facility (ZGT), 2.2-Second Drop Tower.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
## 1. Physical Sciences Overview & Gravity Effects on Combustion
In the United States, combustion processes contribute to approximately 85% of delivered energy and are an integral part in many industrial fabrication processes. However, combustion produces greenhouse gases, soot, and particulate pollutants. Despite over 80 years of active research, combustion remains one of the most difficult phenomena to predict and control because even simple combustors (such as a kitchen gas burner) involve hundreds of intermediate chemical species and thousands of reactions that govern flammability limits and pollutant emissions.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text: On Earth (normal gravity, 1-g), combustion is dominated by buoyant forces. Typical flame temperatures reach ~2,300 K, whereas ambient cabin temperatures are approximately 300 K. This temperature differential produces an eight-fold (8x) density gradient over a spatial scale of just one centimeter. The resulting buoyancy induces a strong upward velocity field that dominates all but the highest forced flow fields. This flow field causes flames to stretch upward, induce flickers, and obscure fundamental chemical kinetics and heat transfer mechanisms.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text: In microgravity (free fall aboard the International Space Station), buoyant convection is suppressed. Flames become spherical, steady, and quiescent, reducing complex three-dimensional convection into one-dimensional spherical diffusion systems that can be analyzed and modeled numerically with high fidelity. Microgravity experimentation provides the foundational science necessary for spacecraft fire safety and material flammability assessment.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
## 2. Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)
- Program Role: First-ever combustion experiment to be performed on another planetary body (the lunar surface at 1/6 g).
- Objective: Investigate burning materials at the Moon's 1/6 reduced gravity level. Computational modeling, drop tower centrifuge tests, and ISS microgravity experiments indicate that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity compared to Earth (1-g). Materials classified as non-flammable under Earth standard tests can become flammable in lunar surface habitats and pressurized rovers.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
- Fuel Samples: Four fuel samples burned individually in atmospheric conditions planned for future lunar habitats and rovers. Key fuel tested is SIBAL fabric (Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speed fabric, a cotton-fiberglass textile blend) in both upward and downward burning configurations.
- Hardware Specifications: Autonomous sealed combustion chamber measuring 28.5 x 28.5 x 38.5 cm with a mass of 25 kg, designed for lunar landers.
- Diagnostics & Sensors: Onboard video cameras recording flame size, color, luminosity, and flame spread rate; onboard thermocouples for flame and fuel surface temperatures; oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration sensors.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text: - Leadership: Principal Investigator Dr. Paul Ferkul (Universities Space Research Association), Co-Investigator Prof. Ya-Ting Liao (Case Western Reserve University), Co-Investigator Dr. Michael Johnston (NASA Glenn Research Center), Project Manager Amber Krauss (NASA Glenn).
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
## 3. Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Project
- Flight Facility: Operating inside the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) within the U.S. Laboratory Module (Destiny) aboard the International Space Station.
- Core Mission: Mitigate catastrophic fire hazards for manned exploration missions. NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 implements an upward flame propagation test in 1-g for flight material screening. However, microgravity research indicates that 1-g testing is not always conservative, as low-speed ventilation and radiation feedback in microgravity can sustain combustion under conditions where 1-g flames extinguish due to buoyant convective heat loss.
- Five Integrated SoFIE Flight Investigations:
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
- Five Integrated SoFIE Flight Investigations:
  1. Residence Time Driven Flame Spread (RTDFS) - PI: Prof. Subrata Bhattacharjee (San Diego State University). Investigates steady vs unsteady flame spread over solid fuels in microgravity. Predicts that steady flame spread cannot be sustained if fuel exceeds a critical thickness due to radiative heat losses, quantified by a non-dimensional radiation parameter proportional to thickness.
  2. Narrow Channel Apparatus (NCA) - PI: Prof. Fletcher Miller (San Diego State University). Measures flame spread across planar PMMA slabs in forced opposed flow. Tested atmospheres range from ambient 21% up to 85% O2 along the normoxic curve across varying flow velocities to map quenching and blowoff extinction boundaries.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
3. Growth and Extinction Limit (GEL) - PI: Prof. James S. T'ien (Case Western Reserve University). Investigates flame growth, decay, and extinction over non-flat thick solids, specifically solid PMMA spheres (4 to 5 cm diameter). Examines unsteady internal heat-up, stagnation point aerodynamics, shoulder, and wake flow regimes.
  4. Material Ignition and Suppression Test (MIST) - PI: Prof. Carlos Fernandez-Pello (UC Berkeley). Consists of a small combustion wind tunnel testing cylindrical fuel samples under radiant heat flux, forced opposed oxidizer flow, and coiled Kanthal wire electrical igniters.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text: 5. Spacecraft Materials Microgravity Research on Flammability (SMuRF) - PI: Dr. Sandra Olson (NASA Glenn Research Center). Establishes quantitative correlations between 1-g flammability screening data and ventilated microgravity flammability, providing verifiable safety margins for spacecraft material selection.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
## 4. Flammability Limits At Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE)
- Multi-Agency International Project: Collaboration among JAXA, NASA, ESA, CNES, and DLR. Flight experiments conducted in the JAXA Kibo Module on the ISS utilizing JAXA's "Solid Combustion" apparatus.
- Science Objective: Develop a predictive correlation methodology that estimates microgravity material flammability limits directly from normal-gravity (1-g) laboratory test data, overcoming limitations of NASA-STD-6001B.
- Mechanism: Elucidates the role of the critical Damköhler number (ratio of flow characteristic time to chemical reaction time, Da = tau_flow / tau_reaction) in controlling solid fuel flame extinction.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text: - Key Investigators: Project Manager Shigeki Kamigaichi (JAXA), Project Scientist Masao Kikuchi (JAXA), JAXA PI Prof. Osamu Fujita (Hokkaido Univ), NASA Co-Is Dr. Sandra Olson (NASA GRC), Dr. Harold Beeson (NASA WSTF), and Prof. Carlos Fernandez-Pello (UC Berkeley).
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
## 5. ISS Combustion Science Facilities
- Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR): Developed by NASA Glenn Research Center, launched to the ISS aboard Space Shuttle Endeavour (STS-126) in November 2008. Located in the U.S. Destiny laboratory, CIR features a 100-liter sealed combustion chamber equipped with multi-wavelength optical diagnostic cameras, gas supply and mixing systems, and automated safety interlocks. CIR is the only rack on ISS dedicated to combustion experimentation.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
- Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA): Modular payload insert for the CIR supporting droplet combustion investigations (including FLEX, FLEX-2, and Cool Flames Investigation CFI). Enables sustained microgravity observation of liquid fuel droplet burning, sooting, radiative extinction, and low-temperature "cool flame" burning regimes.
- Payload Operations: Monitored and commanded 24/7 by the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
## 6. Archived ISS Combustion Science Flight Investigations
- Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME): Focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emissions in practical terrestrial combustion.
- Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS): Examined the burning and extinction characteristics of a wide variety of solid fuel samples in microgravity within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG).
- Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT): Designed to ensure that a modified P-Trak particle counter—a key diagnostic component of the forthcoming SAME experiment—performed properly in the unique environment of microgravity.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
- Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX & FLEX-2): Designed to assess and quantify the effectiveness of inert-gas suppressants (such as CO2 and helium) in microgravity and obtain conservative estimates of the limiting oxygen index (LOI) for steady droplet combustion.
- Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire): Evaluated large-scale material flammability and flame growth in realistic spacecraft architectures inside automated Cygnus resupply vehicles after departing the ISS.
- Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME & SAME-R): Investigated smoke particle morphology and size distributions to improve spacecraft smoke detectors. Demonstrated that hydrocarbon fuels typically produce carbon soot while overheated plastics produce recondensed polymer droplet aerosols.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
- Structure & Liftoff in Combustion Experiment (SLICE): Studied coflow laminar diffusion flames to provide high-precision bench data for detailed numerical kinetics modeling in the absence of buoyant acceleration.
- Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Continued the study of fundamental phenomena controlling the stability, soot generation, and radiative extinction of jet diffusion flames begun with the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) campaign on STS-94.
title: NASA Glenn Combustion Science Program: Physical Sciences Discipline, Facilities & Spacecraft Fire Safety Investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, CIR, MDCA)

text:
# NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study & Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned

Source: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance, Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)
URL: https://sma.nasa.gov/sma-disciplines/accllp/apollo-1
Subject: AS-204 / Apollo 1 Command Module 012 Fire Incident, Technical Investigation, and Institutional Safety Transformation
Date of Incident: January 27, 1967
Location: Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 1. Mission Context & Background
Following the completion of the Gemini program in November 1966, NASA focused on the Apollo program to land astronauts on the Moon. The inaugural crewed Apollo mission was officially designated AS-204 (later formally named Apollo 1 in spring 1967 by NASA Associate Administrator Dr. George E. Mueller). The flight was planned as an open-ended 14-day Earth orbital test flight (up to 330 hours, 50 minutes and 208 revolutions) to qualify the Command and Service Modules (CSM) and the Service Propulsion System (SPS) main engine with eight scheduled test firings.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text: The assigned prime crew consisted of command pilot Virgil "Gus" Grissom (veteran of Mercury-Redstone 4 and Gemini 3), senior pilot Edward H. White II (Gemini 4 veteran and first American spacewalker), and pilot Roger B. Chaffee (spaceflight rookie). The spacecraft assigned to the mission was Command Module 012 (CM-012), a "Block I" design manufactured by North American Aviation in Downey, California. Block I spacecraft were designed for early Earth-orbital qualification, lacking the docking probe and transfer tunnel that characterized the lunar-capable "Block II" spacecraft.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 2. Pre-Launch Testing & Hazard Classification
On January 27, 1967, the crew entered CM-012 atop the Saturn IB rocket at Launch Complex 34 to conduct a critical "plugs-out" simulated countdown test. The test was designed to verify that the spacecraft could operate autonomously on internal battery power with umbilical connections severed.

The spacecraft cabin was sealed and pressurized with 100% pure oxygen at 16.7 pounds per square inch absolute (psia; approximately 115 kPa), which was 2.0 psi above ambient sea-level atmospheric pressure to ensure a positive pressure differential.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
Crucially, because the Saturn IB rocket was unfueled during this simulation, NASA management categorized the test as "non-hazardous." Consequently:
- Emergency pad safety personnel, medical triage, and fire suppression crews were not stationed on the launch gantry.
- No emergency egress equipment or high-pressure water deluge systems were active.
- The launch pad work structure lacked clear escape paths for pad technicians.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 3. The Fire Outbreak & Accident Dynamics
At 6:31:04 p.m. EST, telemetry recorded a voltage surge and crew audio captured cries of fire within the cabin: "Fire! We've got a fire in the cockpit!"
- Ignition Source: The Apollo 204 Review Board determined that the fire was most likely initiated by electrical arcing from damaged or chafed wiring located near the Environmental Control System (ECS) instrumentation below the crew couches.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
- Flashover: In an unvented 100% pure oxygen atmosphere at 16.7 psia, solid materials normally considered flame-resistant on Earth ignited instantly. Combustible materials including nylon netting, flammable Velcro strips (used extensively throughout the cockpit for equipment retention), polyurethane foam, and silicone wire insulation fed a ferocious flash fire that swept through the module in under 15 seconds.
- Pressure Vessel Rupture: Intense heat generated extreme internal gas expansion, causing cabin pressure to exceed 29 psia (200 kPa) within seconds. The Command Module inner aluminum pressure shell ruptured at 6:31:19 p.m., spewing flames, heat, and dense black smoke onto the levels of Launch Complex 34.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text: - Ingress/Egress Trap: The Command Module hatch was a complex three-piece assembly: an inner hatch held in place by internal pressure, an intermediate hatch, and an outer thermal hatch. Under ideal conditions, unlatching the hatch took a minimum of 90 seconds and required special tools. The elevated internal pressure pushed the inward-opening hatch tightly against its seal, making it physically impossible for astronaut Ed White to unlatch or open from the inside.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text: - Medical Finding: Pad technicians wearing inadequate gas masks fought dense toxic fumes and opened the hatch after approximately 5 minutes, but found the astronauts deceased. Autopsies conducted by U.S. Air Force pathologists concluded that the crew perished from acute asphyxiation caused by carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and inhalation of toxic pyrolysis gases. Their third-degree thermal burns occurred posthumously or were deemed secondary and non-lethal on their own.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 4. Apollo 204 Review Board & Congressional Inquiry
On January 28, 1967, Deputy Administrator Robert C. Seamans Jr. established the Apollo 204 Review Board, chaired by Dr. Floyd L. Thompson (Director of NASA Langley Research Center). The board's 3,000-page report, released on April 9, 1967, and subsequent Senate and House hearings led by Senator Clinton P. Anderson and Representative Olin E. Teague, identified systemic engineering defects, severe configuration management lapses, and inadequate safety oversight.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 5. Major Engineering & Spacecraft Redesigns
1. Unified Quick-Release Hatch:
   - The cumbersome 3-piece hatch was completely replaced with a single outward-opening, unified quick-action hatch.
   - The new hatch was equipped with a nitrogen-actuated pneumatic latch mechanism capable of being opened from either inside or outside the cabin in under 3 seconds.
2. Launch Pad Atmosphere Modification:
   - The dangerous 100% pure oxygen ground-testing environment was discontinued.
   - For all ground pre-launch operations, NASA implemented a two-gas mixture: 60% oxygen / 40% nitrogen at sea-level pressure (14.7 psia / 101.3 kPa).
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
- In flight, the spacecraft cabin bled down to 100% pure oxygen at a reduced, safe pressure of 5.0 psia (34.5 kPa), where combustion rates and flammability limits are markedly lower.
3. Total Combustibles Elimination & Material Screening:
   - All flammable nylon, polyurethane, and standard Velcro were stripped from the crew compartment.
   - Non-combustible woven fiberglass Beta cloth, Teflon insulation, and Nomex/PBI (polybenzimidazole) fabrics were introduced for crew flight suits and cabin stowage.
   - NASA established the Materials and Processes Technical Information System and mandated rigorous flammability screening standards (the direct ancestor of NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 for upward flame propagation).
4. Electrical & Environmental Control Hardening:
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
4. Electrical & Environmental Control Hardening:
   - All cabin wiring was re-routed through protective metal conduits and Teflon wraps to prevent chafing, moisture accumulation, and mechanical abrasion.
   - The flammable ethylene glycol coolant loop was redesigned with soldered joints to prevent leakage.
5. Spacecraft Fleet Decision:
   - NASA permanently retired all crewed Block I spacecraft. All subsequent human missions flew exclusively on the heavily redesigned Block II spacecraft.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 6. Safety Culture & Institutional Transformation
The Apollo 1 accident reshaped NASA's institutional structure:
- All high-energy, closed-cabin, or pressurized tests are now classified as hazardous by default, regardless of vehicle fueling status.
- Mandatory independent Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA) authority was instituted across all NASA programs.
- Real-time crew escape protocols, launch pad fire suppression deluges, and rapid-response safety teams were made mandatory for all human spaceflight operations.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 1 (AS-204) Case Study, Investigation, and Spaceflight Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
# NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study & Spacecraft Cryogenic Fire Safety Lessons Learned

Source: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance, Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)
URL: https://sma.nasa.gov/sma-disciplines/accllp/apollo-13
Subject: Apollo 13 (CSM-109 Odyssey / LM-7 Aquarius) Cryogenic Oxygen Tank No. 2 Fire and In-Flight Explosion
Date of Incident: April 13, 1970
Location: Translunar Coast (~200,000 miles from Earth)
Vehicle: Apollo Command and Service Module (CSM-109 Odyssey) and Lunar Module (LM-7 Aquarius)
Crew: James A. Lovell Jr. (Commander), John L. "Jack" Swigert Jr. (Command Module Pilot), Fred W. Haise Jr. (Lunar Module Pilot)
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 1. Mission Objectives & Pre-Launch Anomalies
Apollo 13 was scheduled as the third crewed lunar landing, targeted for the rugged Fra Mauro highlands. Days prior to launch, backup Lunar Module Pilot Charles Duke inadvertently exposed the prime crew to rubella (German measles). Because prime Command Module Pilot Ken Mattingly lacked immunity, backup CMP Jack Swigert was substituted 72 hours before liftoff.

During launch on April 11, 1970, the Saturn V S-II second stage center J-2 engine shut down 2 minutes early due to severe pogo oscillations. The remaining four outer engines burned 34 seconds longer and the S-IVB third stage burned 9 seconds longer to successfully achieve low Earth parking orbit, and translunar injection proceeded normally.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 2. In-Flight Explosion & Spacecraft Emergency
At 55 hours and 55 minutes Ground Elapsed Time (April 13, 1970), roughly 200,000 miles from Earth, the crew completed a 49-minute televised broadcast. Shortly thereafter, Mission Control requested that CMP Jack Swigert activate the cryogenic oxygen and hydrogen tank stirring fans to destratify the fluids for accurate quantity readouts.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
Within seconds:
- A dull bang vibrated through the spacecraft structure, accompanied by a high-gain antenna oscillation and telemetry glitch.
- Master alarms sounded as two of the three main electrical fuel cells died.
- Jack Swigert radioed: "Houston, we've had a problem here."
- Approximately 14 minutes later, Commander Jim Lovell looked through the Command Module window and reported: "We are venting something out into the... into space... It's a gas of some sort."
- Cryogenic Oxygen Tank No. 2 had ruptured, and the concussive burst or shrapnel damaged the adjacent Oxygen Tank No. 1 or its plumbing. With oxygen rapidly escaping into the vacuum, all three fuel cells died, depleting electrical power and drinking/cooling water generation.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 3. "Lifeboat" Operations & Critical Survival Hurdles
With only 15 minutes of electrical battery reserve remaining in the mortally wounded Command Module Odyssey, Flight Director Eugene F. Kranz and the Mission Control team ordered the crew into the Lunar Module Aquarius to serve as an emergency "lifeboat":
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text: - Carbon Dioxide Removal: Aquarius was designed to support two astronauts for two days on the Moon, not three astronauts for four days. The square lithium hydroxide (LiOH) canisters from the CM were incompatible with the round openings of the LM environmental system. Ground engineers at the Manned Spacecraft Center designed a jerry-rigged adapter constructed from flight-plan cardboard covers, spacesuit hoses, plastic collection bags, and grey duct tape ("the mailbox"), reducing cabin CO2 to safe levels.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
- Thermal & Water Depletion: To preserve electrical power for reentry, Aquarius was powered down to bare minimal avionics (~12% power draw). Cabin temperatures plunged to 38°F (3.3°C), causing dense condensation to form on all cold metal instrument panels and bulkheads. The crew restricted water intake to 6 ounces per day (1/5 of standard rations) to preserve water for equipment cooling sublimation.
- Cold Reentry Power-Up (Apollo 1 Synergy): Re-energizing the drenched Command Module electronics prior to atmospheric entry carried acute risks of electrical short-circuiting. The power-up was successful solely because the wiring had been upgraded with waterproof insulation and protective sealed conduits as a direct corrective action following the 1967 Apollo 1 fire.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 4. Technical Root Cause & Review Board Findings (Edgar M. Cortright Report)
The Apollo 13 Review Board, established by NASA Administrator Thomas O. Paine and chaired by NASA Langley Director Edgar M. Cortright, determined that the accident stemmed from a 5-year chain of engineering oversights:
1. Incompatible Voltage Upgrade (1965): Ground heater power specifications were increased from 28 VDC to 65 VDC to expedite detanking on the launch pad. However, the subcontracted thermostatic disconnect switches inside the tanks were overlooked and remained rated for only 28 VDC.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text: 2. Launch Pad Thermal Damage: During a Countdown Demonstration Test (CDT) at KSC in March 1970, Tank No. 2 could not be emptied through its normal drain tube. Technicians activated the tank internal heaters for an continuous 8-hour period to boil out the liquid oxygen. The 28-volt thermostatic switches welded shut under the 65-volt supply, allowing heater tube temperatures to reach an estimated 1,000°F (538°C).
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text: 3. Supercritical Oxygen Combustion: The prolonged 1,000°F heat severely degraded the Teflon insulation on the stirring fan wiring. When Swigert activated the cryo-stirrer in transit, an electrical arc ignited the bare wire inside pure supercritical oxygen (>700 psia / 4.8 MPa). The Teflon insulation burned rapidly, causing pressure to rise above 1,000 psi in seconds, rupturing the tank dome and blowing off Service Module Sector 4 exterior panel.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned
authors: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
Apollo Case Studies and Lessons Learned Program (ACCLLP)

text:
## 5. Engineering Redesigns & Cryogenic Safety Mandates (Apollo 14+)
1. Isolated Cryogenic Storage:
   - A third cryogenic oxygen tank was installed in an entirely isolated bay (Bay 1) separated by a structural barrier from Tanks 1 and 2, ensuring single-point shrapnel cannot cause total loss of consumables.
2. Removal of Submerged Motors:
   - Internal stirring fan motors were completely removed from all cryogenic oxygen vessels. Destratification was achieved without moving parts inside pure oxygen.
3. Electrical Hardening:
   - All internal heater and sensor wiring inside cryogenic tanks was sheathed in protective stainless steel conduit.
   - Thermostatic switches were upgraded to 65 VDC compatibility and equipped with redundant over-temperature limiters.
title: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance (SMA): Apollo 13 Case Study, Cryogenic Fire Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons Learned

4. Auxiliary Emergency Reserves:
   - Added an auxiliary 400-amp-hour battery and dedicated 40-pound auxiliary water reservoir inside the Command Module for emergency entry power.

text:
# NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

Source: NASA History Office / Johnson Space Center (Author: John Uri)
URL: https://www.nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir/
Date Published: February 23, 2022
Date of Incident: February 23–24, 1997
Location: Kvant-1 Module, Russian Space Station Mir
Vehicle & Mission: Mir EO-22/EO-23 Handover & NASA-4 Joint Flight
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

text:
## 1. Context and Handover Crew
In February 1997, the Russian space station Mir accommodated a six-person handover crew:
- Resident Expedition 22 crew: Valeri G. Korzun (Commander, Roscosmos), Aleksandr Y. Kaleri (Flight Engineer, Roscosmos), and Dr. Jerry M. Linenger (NASA Astronaut, arrived via Space Shuttle Atlantis STS-81 in January 1997).
- Newly-arrived Expedition 23 crew: Vasili V. Tsibliyev (Commander, Roscosmos), Aleksandr I. Lazutkin (Flight Engineer, Roscosmos), and Reinhold Ewald (Astronaut, German Space Agency DLR).
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

text:
Under standard operations with three crew members, oxygen was generated using two "Elektron" water-electrolysis units that split reclaimed water into oxygen and hydrogen. When crew size grew to six during handovers, the station utilized supplementary Solid Fuel Oxygen Generators (SFOG), known as "Vika" or by the Russian acronym "TGK."

## 2. The Oxygen Generator Failure and Flame Dynamics
Each SFOG canister contained solid lithium perchlorate (LiClO4) that chemically generated oxygen through thermal decomposition, providing enough oxygen to support one crew member per day. The system had been utilized without incident over 2,500 times aboard Mir and for decades on submarines.
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

text:
Shortly after dinner on February 23/24, 1997, as cosmonaut Aleksandr Lazutkin activated an SFOG canister in Mir’s Kvant-1 module, the unit burst into flames:
- Flame Profile: A searing, three-foot blowtorch-like chemical flame shot across the narrow Kvant-1 module, spraying molten metal droplets, sparks, and dense toxic smoke.
- Evacuation Route Blockage: The chemical flame physically blocked the passageway to one of the two docked Soyuz escape vehicles (the spacecraft designated for Korzun, Kaleri, and Ewald), eliminating the possibility of emergency evacuation for half the crew.
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

text:
- Firefighting in Microgravity: Because discharging a fire extinguisher in microgravity exerts an equal opposite reaction force that throws the firefighter backwards, NASA astronaut Jerry Linenger physically anchored and held cosmonaut Valeri Korzun in place while Korzun aimed foam extinguishers directly into the combustion core. The crew exhausted three pressurized foam fire extinguishers to contain the blaze and cool adjacent structural bulkheads until the chemical reaction burned out.
- Smoke & Life Support: Dense toxic smoke enveloped Mir's interconnected modules. The crew donned oxygen masks and respirators, and the environmental control system scrubbed the atmosphere of toxic pyrolysis gases over several hours.
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

text:
## 3. Two-Year Technical Root Cause Investigation
The charred remains of the SFOG canister were returned to Earth aboard a NASA Space Shuttle mission for forensic analysis.
- Following a two-year investigation, engineers determined that hydrocarbon contaminants had entered the canister during assembly.
- Forensic pathologists and engineers identified the primary contaminant as latex particles from working gloves inadvertently introduced during ground packaging, which reacted violently with the heated lithium perchlorate oxidizer.
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

text:
## 4. Engineering Lessons Learned & International Space Station (ISS) Architecture
The Mir fire represented the worst in-orbit fire in spaceflight history and directly transformed spaceflight fire safety design on the International Space Station:
1. Dissimilar Redundant Life Support:
   - The ISS abandoned sole reliance on chemical candles. The primary oxygen architecture uses redundant water-electrolysis systems: three upgraded Elektron units in the Russian Zvezda module and the American Oxygen Generation System (OGS) in the Destiny laboratory.
   - SFOG canisters serve strictly as a tertiary backup with rigorous ground cleanroom manufacturing standards excluding all hydrocarbon and latex contaminants.
2. Microgravity Fire Suppression:
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

text:
2. Microgravity Fire Suppression:
   - Prompted development and deployment of fine-water-mist fire extinguishers on the ISS, which extinguish intense fires without filling enclosed microgravity modules with toxic chemical residues or causing asphyxiation.
3. Firefighter Restraints and Access:
   - Established mandatory microgravity foot restraints and handholds near high-risk equipment bays so crew members can discharge extinguishers without being propelled backward.
4. Rapid Ventilation Isolation:
   - Engineered automated ventilation shutoffs to isolate any single module, cutting off convective oxidizer flow and preventing smoke propagation into emergency escape vehicles.
title: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Incident Dynamics, Forensic Investigation, and Spacecraft Fire Safety Lessons

# NASA Spinoff: Lightweight Firefighter Breathing Apparatus & High-Pressure Composite Air Tanks

Source: NASA Spinoff Technology Transfer Program (Node 9582) / NASA Johnson Space Center
URL: https://spinoff.nasa.gov/node/9582
Publication Record: NASA Spinoff 1976 / NASA Technical Report hdl:2060/20030005480 / NTRS 19760020150
Commercial Partner: Scott Aviation (division of A-T-O Inc.), Structural Composites Inc., The Boeing Co., Martin-Marietta Corp.
Origin Center: NASA Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center (JSC), Houston, Texas
title: NASA Spinoff: Lightweight Firefighter Breathing Apparatus & High-Pressure Composite Air Tanks (Spacecraft Life Support Technology Transfer)

text:
## 1. Spaceflight Origin & Engineering Need
During the Apollo and early Space Shuttle programs, NASA engineers at Johnson Space Center developed filament-wound composite pressure vessels for astronaut Portable Life Support Systems (PLSS) and spacecraft auxiliary propulsion tanks. These containers required ultra-high pressure storage (4,500 psi to 6,000 psi) capable of enduring high vibration and zero-leak tolerances while minimizing launch mass.
title: NASA Spinoff: Lightweight Firefighter Breathing Apparatus & High-Pressure Composite Air Tanks (Spacecraft Life Support Technology Transfer)

text:
In the 1970s, conventional municipal firefighter Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) systems relied on heavy, low-pressure steel cylinders. A standard 30-minute air bottle weighed upwards of 33 pounds (15 kg), significantly hindering firefighter mobility, contributing to heat stress, exhaustion, and heart attacks—the leading cause of on-duty firefighter fatalities.

## 2. NASA Technology Transfer & Breakthrough Commercialization
Under a joint initiative between NASA Johnson Space Center and the National Bureau of Standards (NBS), NASA partnered with Scott Aviation (A-T-O Inc.) and composite fabricators (Structural Composites Inc., Boeing, Martin-Marietta) to transfer spaceflight pressure vessel technology to municipal fire departments.
title: NASA Spinoff: Lightweight Firefighter Breathing Apparatus & High-Pressure Composite Air Tanks (Spacecraft Life Support Technology Transfer)

text:
Key technological innovations transferred from space exploration:
1. Lightweight Composite Construction:
   - Replaced solid steel cylinders with a seamless aluminum alloy inner liner overwrapped with resin-impregnated high-strength fiberglass filament.
   - Reduced total backpack weight from 33 pounds down to just 20 pounds for a standard 30-minute air supply—saving 13 pounds (a 40% mass reduction).
   - Eliminated internal rust and condensation-induced cylinder corrosion.
2. Doubled Operating Pressure:
   - Increased cylinder pressure rating from the legacy 2,216 psi to 4,500 psi (over double conventional pressures), providing a full 30-minute air supply in a significantly smaller, more maneuverable envelope.
3. Ergonomic Harness & Apollo PLSS Backpack Frame:
title: NASA Spinoff: Lightweight Firefighter Breathing Apparatus & High-Pressure Composite Air Tanks (Spacecraft Life Support Technology Transfer)

text:
3. Ergonomic Harness & Apollo PLSS Backpack Frame:
   - Re-engineered the cylinder harness based on Apollo spacesuit backpack human-factors research. 
   - Shifted cylinder mass off the firefighter's upper shoulders and onto the hips, vastly improving mobility and center of gravity when climbing ladders or crawling through collapsed structures.
4. Redesigned Wide-Vision Mask & Personalized Low-Air Warning:
   - Designed a new panoramic-vision silicone facepiece minimizing fogging and peripheral blind spots.
   - Integrated a personalized low-air acoustic warning whistle/vibrator tuned specifically so only the individual firefighter hears it, preventing confusion with nearby teammates' alarms in smoky, chaotic fire environments.
title: NASA Spinoff: Lightweight Firefighter Breathing Apparatus & High-Pressure Composite Air Tanks (Spacecraft Life Support Technology Transfer)

text:
## 3. Global Public Safety Impact & PSI Synergy
The NASA-developed lightweight composite SCBA tank was formally adopted by the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) under NFPA 1981 standards and has become standard life-safety equipment for hundreds of thousands of municipal, industrial, and wildfire firefighters worldwide.

In microgravity combustion and spacecraft fire safety science (NASA PSI / ISS), the principles of high-pressure composite gas containment, breathable gas management, and non-toxic atmospheric life support continue to evolve directly from this aerospace-terrestrial lineage.
title: NASA Spinoff: Lightweight Firefighter Breathing Apparatus & High-Pressure Composite Air Tanks (Spacecraft Life Support Technology Transfer)

# NASA Spinoff: Incipient Fire Detector & Combustion Particle vs. Dust Discrimination

Source: NASA Spinoff Technology Transfer Program (Node 9407) / NASA Space Shuttle Orbiter Program
URL: https://spinoff.nasa.gov/node/9407
Publication Record: NASA Spinoff 1978 / NASA Technical Report hdl:2060/20070018916
Commercial Technology: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Brunswick Corporation)
Origin Program: NASA Space Shuttle Orbiter Life Support & Fire Detection System
title: NASA Spinoff: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Space Shuttle Combustion Particle vs Dust Discrimination)

text:
## 1. Spaceflight Origin & Engineering Need
In human spaceflight, early fire detection is vital because enclosed spacecraft cabins lack natural buoyant exhaust, allowing toxic pyrolysis products and heat to accumulate rapidly in confined volumes. For the Space Shuttle orbiter fleet, NASA required a detector capable of identifying overheated electronics, pyrolyzing wire insulation, and smoldering materials long before visible smoke or open flame appeared.

Furthermore, microgravity environments cause cabin lint, payload particulates, and dust to float indefinitely rather than settling to the floor as they do on Earth. Conventional terrestrial optical smoke detectors triggered unacceptable false alarms in the presence of airborne dust, creating dangerous operational disruptions.
title: NASA Spinoff: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Space Shuttle Combustion Particle vs Dust Discrimination)

text:
## 2. NASA Technology Transfer & Breakthrough Commercialization
To solve this challenge, NASA partnered with the Brunswick Corporation to engineer the Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector for the Space Shuttle orbiters.
title: NASA Spinoff: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Space Shuttle Combustion Particle vs Dust Discrimination)

text:
Key technological innovations:
1. Particle Discrimination (Smoke vs. Dust):
   - Rather than simply measuring optical obscuration, the system continuously samples ambient cabin air through an ionization/condensation chamber that analyzes particle size distributions.
   - It reliably discriminates between sub-micron combustion particles (produced during early pyrolysis) and larger extraneous matter such as airborne mineral dust, lint, and humidity aerosols.
   - This eliminates the chronic false-alarm vulnerabilities that plagued legacy detectors.
2. Incipient Warning Prior to Visible Flame:
   - Signals the presence of a developing fire condition minutes before the emergence of open flames, high heat, or visible smoke plumes.
title: NASA Spinoff: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Space Shuttle Combustion Particle vs Dust Discrimination)

text:
- Enables operators to depower compromised electrical circuits before catastrophic thermal runaway occurs.
3. Networked Central Fire Watch Architecture:
   - Adapted for large-scale industrial and hazardous subterranean applications, including underground coal and metal mines.
   - Multiple distributed sampling sensors are connected to a centralized processor and display console, instantly warning safety managers of incipient thermal events and pinpointing the exact hazard location across extensive facility ductwork.
title: NASA Spinoff: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Space Shuttle Combustion Particle vs Dust Discrimination)

text:
## 3. Terrestrial Public Safety Impact & PSI Synergy
The technology transferred from the Space Shuttle's Brunswick detector became the foundational architecture for modern aspirating smoke detection (ASD) systems utilized worldwide in semiconductor fabrication cleanrooms, telecommunications data centers, transit tunnels, and underground mining operations.
title: NASA Spinoff: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Space Shuttle Combustion Particle vs Dust Discrimination)

text:
In microgravity combustion research, this lineage directly informs modern ISS experiments:
- The Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME and SAME-R) investigated microgravity smoke particle morphology and aging.
- The Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT and DAFT-2) adapted this instrumentation to measure lunar regolith simulant and cabin dust, directly completing the circle between terrestrial mine safety and lunar base habitat protection.
title: NASA Spinoff: Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector (Space Shuttle Combustion Particle vs Dust Discrimination)

# NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES - Advanced Protective Firefighter Turnout Gear & Thermal Materials

Source: NASA Spinoff Technology Transfer Program (Node 9918) / NASA Marshall Space Flight Center
URL: https://spinoff.nasa.gov/node/9918
Publication Record: NASA Spinoff 1982 / NASA Technical Report hdl:2060/20030002834 / NTRS 19780004514
Sponsoring Agencies: NASA & Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) / U.S. Fire Administration (USFA)
Technical Management: NASA George C. Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC), Huntsville, Alabama
Program Initiative: Project FIRES (Firefighter's Integrated Response Equipment System)
title: NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES - Firefighter Integrated Response Equipment System (Apollo Space Suit Materials Transfer)

text:
## 1. Spaceflight Origin & Engineering Need
Following the 1967 Apollo 1 launch pad fire, NASA embarked on an intensive materials development campaign to engineer non-flammable polymers, thermal barriers, and composite textile assemblies for astronaut Extravehicular Activity (EVA) spacesuits and spacecraft command module interiors. NASA developed and qualified materials such as woven fiberglass Beta cloth, polybenzimidazole (PBI), Nomex, and Kevlar that resist open flame impingement, withstand temperatures exceeding 500°C (932°F) without melting or dripping, and provide lightweight thermal insulation.
title: NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES - Firefighter Integrated Response Equipment System (Apollo Space Suit Materials Transfer)

text: In the 1970s, municipal firefighters faced severe risks of burns, heat stroke, and toxic smoke exposure due to obsolete turnout gear made of heavy rubberized coats, canvas, and wool. These legacy materials absorbed extreme heat, lacked moisture vapor breathability, and melted or burned during flashover incidents.
title: NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES - Firefighter Integrated Response Equipment System (Apollo Space Suit Materials Transfer)

text:
## 2. NASA Technology Transfer: Project FIRES
To curb firefighter casualties, NASA joined forces with the U.S. Fire Administration (USFA) under FEMA to launch Project FIRES (Firefighter's Integrated Response Equipment System), directed by NASA Marshall Space Flight Center:
1. Aerospace Thermal Ensemble:
   - Transferred advanced lightweight, fire-resistant, and heat-protective materials originally engineered for Apollo astronaut spacesuits and spacecraft thermal protection systems.
   - Incorporated multi-layer thermal architectures: high-strength flame-resistant outer shells (PBI/Kevlar blends), moisture barriers preventing scalding steam burns, and thermal liners trapping insulating air.
2. 14-City Municipal Field Evaluation:
title: NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES - Firefighter Integrated Response Equipment System (Apollo Space Suit Materials Transfer)

text:
2. 14-City Municipal Field Evaluation:
   - Manufactured complete FIRES prototype protective ensembles (turnout coats, bunker pants, boots, helmets, and gloves) and conducted exhaustive live-fire evaluations with 14 municipal fire departments across the United States.
   - Evaluated mobility, heat stress reduction, tear resistance, and flashover survivability under actual firefighting conditions.
3. Creation of Nationwide Firefighter Protective Standards:
   - Field test data from Project FIRES formed the empirical foundation for modern national fire protection standards, establishing the framework for NFPA 1971 (Standard on Protective Ensembles for Structural Fire Fighting).
title: NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES - Firefighter Integrated Response Equipment System (Apollo Space Suit Materials Transfer)

text:
## 3. Global Public Safety Impact & PSI Synergy
Project FIRES transformed civilian structural firefighting globally, drastically decreasing second- and third-degree burn casualties, steam scalds, and heat-exhaustion incidents.

In microgravity combustion and spacecraft fire safety science (NASA PSI / ISS):
- Investigations like BASS, BASS-II, and Saffire evaluate flame spread over aerospace fabrics and solid materials, continuously feeding into the flammability limits (NASA-STD-6001) that govern both orbital space stations and civilian firefighter protective gear on Earth.
title: NASA Spinoff: Project FIRES - Firefighter Integrated Response Equipment System (Apollo Space Suit Materials Transfer)

text: # A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
Document ID: NASA/NP-2015-10-034-JSC
Publication Date: October 2015 Edition (Published July 2016)
Organization: NASA International Space Station (ISS) Program Science Office / Space Station Research Integration Office
Authors:
- Suleyman A. Gokoglu, Ph.D. (NASA Glenn Research Center)
- Daniel L. Dietrich, Ph.D. (NASA Glenn Research Center)
- Dennis P. Stocker (NASA Glenn Research Center)
- Paul V. Ferkul, Ph.D. (Universities Space Research Association - USRA)
- Sandy L. Olson, Ph.D. (NASA Glenn Research Center)
- Michael C. Hicks, Ph.D. (NASA Glenn Research Center)
Source URL: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science/
PDF Reference: NP-2015-10-034-JSC (ISS Mini-Book Series)

---
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
---

## 1. Executive Summary & Microgravity Combustion Rationale
Combustion provides approximately 85% of delivered energy on Earth across transportation, electric power generation, and materials manufacturing (steel, glass). However, combustion processes produce soot, particulate matter, and greenhouse emissions, and remain among the most complex multi-scale physical phenomena.

On Earth (1-g), combustion is dominated by buoyancy-driven natural convection. High flame temperatures (~2,300 K) adjacent to cool ambient air (~300 K) produce steep eight-fold (8x) density gradients over spatial scales of less than one centimeter. The resulting buoyancy generates strong upward velocities that mask chemical kinetics, soot inception, and molecular transport mechanisms.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station (ISS):
- Buoyancy-driven natural convection is virtually eliminated (residual acceleration levels 10^-6 to 10^-4 g).
- Convective stretch and flickering are suppressed, allowing flames to assume steady, spherical, one-dimensional symmetry.
- Characteristic transport times increase by orders of magnitude, shifting combustion regimes into diffusion-controlled, low-stretch zones where long-residence-time chemical pathways (such as cool flames and low-temperature oxidation) can be observed and isolated.
- The simplified geometry enables direct, high-fidelity quantitative validation of chemical kinetic mechanisms and numerical combustion codes.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text: - It provides realistic operational simulations of fire hazards, flammability limits, and suppression dynamics in human exploration spacecraft and planetary habitats.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
---

## 2. Spacecraft Fire Safety: Three Critical Fallacies & Corrective Principles
NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) investigations across drop towers, parabolic aircraft, space shuttle missions, and the ISS have overturned three historical misconceptions that previously compromised spacecraft fire safety architectures:
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Fallacy 1: "A steady fire cannot exist in a quiescent microgravity environment."
- **Experimental Reality:** While high-burning-rate terrestrial flames starve without forced convection, microgravity diffusion flames can establish spherical, steady, or slowly expanding reaction fronts that persist for extended durations in quiescent air, drawing sufficient oxidizer through molecular diffusion.
- **Smoldering Risk:** Porous materials (e.g., upholstery, foam insulation, wiring bundles) can sustain low-temperature smoldering combustion for hours in quiescent or near-quiescent microgravity, emitting copious toxic gases without producing a detectable open flame or thermal plume.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Fallacy 2: "A fire will self-extinguish if spacecraft cabin ventilation is shut off."
- **Experimental Reality:** Halting environmental ventilation (shutting down cabin air ducts) eliminates forced airflow but does not immediately extinguish fires. Oxygen diffusion continues to support smoldering or low-intensity burning.
- **Secondary Flashover Hazard:** When ventilation or cabin pressure differentials are restored during post-event response or crew movement, fresh airflow entrainment into heated, fuel-rich pyrolyzate zones can trigger sudden, violent flashovers.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Fallacy 3: "Because reduced gravity suppresses buoyancy, terrestrial 1-g fire safety tests (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) represent a very conservative safety standard."
- **Experimental Reality:** In 1-g upward flammability screening (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), strong buoyant convection accelerates heat loss from the flame zone to the environment. In microgravity, the absence of buoyant convective cooling, coupled with slow forced flows (such as cabin ventilation at 0.05 to 0.2 m/s), prolongs residence time and maintains radiative thermal feedback.
- **Consequence:** Materials rated as self-extinguishing or non-flammable under standard 1-g test protocols can sustain vigorous flame spread in microgravity under low-speed concurrent or opposed forced airflow.

---
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
---

## 3. Advanced Spacecraft Fire Protection Systems (Detection & Suppression)
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Fire Detection & Particulate Diagnostics
- **Smoke Aerosol Physics:** Terrestrial smoke detectors rely on small, buoyancy-sheared smoke particles (~0.1 to 0.3 μm). In microgravity, the prolonged residence time and lack of convective shear promote particulate agglomeration, resulting in significantly larger smoke particles (up to several micrometers). Standard terrestrial ionization and optical detectors experience delayed response or false triggers when deployed in space.
- **Flight Validations:**
  - *DAFT (Dust Aerosol Feasibility Test):* Quantified background cabin dust and aerosol particulate baselines on the ISS.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
- *SAME (Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment):* Measured particle-size distributions from spacecraft material pyrolysis, establishing calibration standards for next-generation orbital smoke sensors.
  - *Multi-Signature Detectors:* GRC developed combined particulate and chemical species sensors (monitoring CO, CO2, and particle sizes simultaneously), which were evaluated with the FAA and demonstrated superior false-alarm rejection and faster real-event detection than commercial aviation detectors.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Fire Suppression & Halon Replacements
- **Water Mist Extinguishers:** Originating from the STS-107 *Mist* experiment (Colorado School of Mines / T. McKinnon), NASA developed non-toxic, fine-droplet water-mist portable fire extinguishers. These extinguish fires through rapid thermal droplet vaporization, latent heat extraction, and oxygen dilution without the toxic or asphyxiant risks of legacy carbon dioxide (CO2) or Halon systems. The first two flight units were delivered to the ISS in December 2015 to replace CO2 units.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text: - **Suppression Hydrodynamics in Microgravity:** In the absence of buoyancy, extinguisher suppressant jets must be directed with caution. In microgravity, a high-velocity jet (e.g., pure nitrogen or gaseous suppressant) applied to a wake-stabilized or obstructed flame can entrain ambient oxygen into the pyrolyzing core, inadvertently intensifying the flame rather than extinguishing it.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
---

## 4. Major Flight Combustion Research Projects & Facilities
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Droplet Combustion & The FLEX Experiments
- **Facility:** Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) inside the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).
- **Project:** Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX / FLEX-2 / FLEX-ICE-GA). Tested hydrocarbon droplets (n-heptane, n-octane, n-decane, methanol, ethanol) between 1 mm and 5 mm diameter in oxygen-inert environments (diluted with N2, CO2, He, Xe) at 0 to 3 atm.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text: - **Cool Flame Discovery:** In 2012, FLEX discovered that after the visible, hot droplet flame extinguished radiatively (T ~ 1,500-2,000 K), the fuel droplet continued to vaporize and burn in an invisible, low-temperature "cool flame" regime (T ~ 600-800 K) driven by low-temperature alkylperoxy chemical kinetics. This revolutionized hydrocarbon combustion theory and opened new pathways for terrestrial clean internal-combustion engine designs.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Gaseous Diffusion Flames & ACME
- **Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME):** Suite of five modular investigations hosted in the CIR:
  1. *BRE (Burning Rate Emulator):* Evaluates condensed fuel flammability and gaseous fuel flow emulation to determine extinction boundaries in low and partial gravity for spacecraft safety.
  2. *CLD Flame (Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame):* Examines soot formation and dilution effects.
  3. *E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames):* Investigates ion generation and electric field control of soot and flame stability.
  4. *Flame Design:* Evaluates stoichiometric optimization and soot suppression via spherical microgravity burner designs.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
5. *s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames):* Measures radiative extinction and chemical kinetic instabilities in spherical diffusion flames using H2, CH4, and C2H4 fuels.
- **SLICE (Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment):** Executed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the SPICE burner, characterizing flame liftoff and stabilization dynamics in low-stretch environments.
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
### Solid Fuel Combustion & Materials Flammability
- **BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) & BASS-II:** Conducted in the MSG. Burned planar slabs, rods, and fabric fuels (PMMA, POM, cotton-fiberglass) under opposed and concurrent airflow (0 to 30 cm/s). Demonstrated that solid materials burn more vigorously under low forced ventilation in microgravity than in 1-g buoyant flow. Tested gaseous nitrogen suppression dynamics.
- **SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction):** CIR-based research initiative encompassing 5 flight investigations:
  - *RTDFS (Residence Time Driven Flame Spread):* Critical fuel thickness and radiative heat loss scaling.
  - *NCA (Narrow Channel Apparatus):* Opposed-flow flame spread over PMMA slabs in Space Exploration Atmospheres (SEA).
title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Space Station Research Integration)

text:
- *GEL (Growth and Extinction Limit):* Spherical fuel geometry flame dynamics.

title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
## Personnel & Collaborating Institutions
- Principal Investigator (PI): Dr. Tanvir I. Farouk (University of South Carolina, Department of Mechanical Engineering)
- NASA Project Scientist: Dr. Michael C. Hicks (NASA Glenn Research Center)
- Key Co-Investigators / Collaborators:

---
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
---

## 1. Investigation Overview & Research Rationale
Under terrestrial (1-g) conditions, buoyant natural convection obscures low-temperature oxidation regimes by stretching the flame zone and accelerating convective heat losses. The microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) suppresses buoyancy, enabling the observation of isolated, spherically symmetric droplet combustion.
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text: During the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), researchers discovered that isolated alkane fuel droplets do not simply extinguish when their luminous hot flame disappears. Instead, after visible flame radiative extinction (at temperatures ~1,500-2,000 K), the droplets continue to vaporize and burn in an invisible, low-temperature "cool flame" regime governed by low-temperature chemical kinetics (temperatures ~600-800 K).
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
However, historical FLEX flight data exhibited unexplained run-to-run variability in droplet burning rates, extinction diameters, and cool flame lifetimes. Investigation PSI-117 was funded to systematically analyze the archived ISS FLEX flight data within the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and deploy advanced multi-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling to resolve whether these variations were caused by external thermal perturbations or unintended microgravity convective drift.

---
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
---

## 2. Research Hypothesis & Computational Methodology
### Primary Hypothesis
External thermo-convective perturbations—specifically imposed spatial temperature gradients, non-uniform radiative heating, and low-speed oscillatory/shear inflows (such as residual vehicle g-jitter or slow cabin ventilation)—govern cool-flame ignition, oscillatory burning, transitions to hot flame re-ignition, and final extinction by altering local residence times and scalar dissipation rates. In microgravity, where natural buoyancy is suppressed, low-speed convective forcing becomes the dominant transport mechanism.
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
### Multi-Physics CFD Modeling Framework (OpenFOAM)
- **Numerical Solver:** Developed within the open-source OpenFOAM platform, solving the full, three-dimensional, variable-density Navier-Stokes equations coupled with energy, species mass fractions, and radiative transport.
- **Low-Temperature Kinetic Schemes:** Incorporated detailed and skeletal chemical mechanisms capturing low-temperature alkylperoxy (RO2) radical formation, isomerization, second oxygen addition (O2 + QOOH -> OOQOOH), and ketohydroperoxide decomposition pathways characteristic of the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) regime.
- **Physical Coupling:**
  - Multi-component heat and mass transfer with non-ideal fluid properties.
  - Participating media radiation (gas-phase H2O and CO2 emission/absorption).
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
- Participating media radiation (gas-phase H2O and CO2 emission/absorption).
  - Preferential vaporization dynamics for multi-component hydrocarbon mixtures.
- **Forcing Modes Evaluated:**
  1. *Convective Perturbation Alone:* Modeled low-speed opposed and cross-flow velocities ($u \sim 0.1$ to $5$ cm/s) representing free-floating droplet drift in the CIR chamber.
  2. *Thermal Perturbation Alone:* Imposed external radiant heat fluxes and chamber wall temperature non-uniformities.
  3. *Combined Thermo-Convective Perturbations:* Simultaneous convective drift and asymmetric heat flux.
  4. *Droplet Dimensional Regimes:* Investigated both large flight-scale droplets ($d_0 = 1.0$ to $4.0$ mm) and sub-millimeter droplets ($d_0 \sim 0.5$ mm) relevant to industrial sprays.
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)
NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
## 3. Key Findings & Quantitative Results
1. **Resolution of FLEX Run-to-Run Variability:**
   - Numerical simulations revealed that even minute convective drift velocities ($< 1$ cm/s), previously deemed negligible in microgravity, produce significant asymmetric shifts in scalar dissipation.
   - Droplet drift distorts the spherical cool flame shell into an ellipsoidal or wake-stabilized front, altering fuel vaporization rates and shifting the final extinction diameter ($D_{ext}$).
2. **Three-Stage Combustion & Cool Flame Persistence:**
   - Documented the transition mechanics across three distinct combustion stages:
     - Stage 1: High-temperature luminous diffusive burning (hot flame, $T \sim 1,500-1,900$ K).
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
- Stage 1: High-temperature luminous diffusive burning (hot flame, $T \sim 1,500-1,900$ K).
     - Stage 2: Radiative extinction of the hot flame followed by transition into a quasi-steady, invisible cool flame ($T \sim 600-800$ K).
     - Stage 3: Second extinction (cool flame extinction) when the droplet diameter reaches the critical extinction diameter $D_{ext}$, or re-ignition to a hot flame under specific convective-thermal conditions.
3. **Oscillatory Cool Flame Dynamics:**
   - Identified near-limit oscillatory cool flame burning under specific low Damköhler number regimes, where the cool flame periodically breathes and oscillates in diameter before either stabilizing or undergoing abrupt kinetic quenching.
4. **Extinction Diameter ($D_{ext}$) Scaling & Pressure Dependence:**
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
4. **Extinction Diameter ($D_{ext}$) Scaling & Pressure Dependence:**
   - Generated precise empirical-computational datasets for n-alkane droplets (n-heptane, n-octane, n-decane, n-dodecane C12).
   - Determined that extinction diameter increases with ambient pressure from 1 atm to 5 atm due to changes in optical thickness and chemical reaction time scales.
5. **Preferential Vaporization in Jet Fuel Surrogates:**
   - Demonstrated that multi-component fuels undergo differential distillation during the cool flame stage: more volatile components (e.g., n-heptane, iso-octane) vaporize preferentially early in the burn, altering the local stoichiometry and chemical reactivity in the cool flame zone.
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)
NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
## 4. Spacecraft Fire Safety Implications
The discoveries from PSI-117 have direct and vital ramifications for crewed spacecraft fire safety architectures:
- **Low-Temperature Fire Hazard Recognition:** Fire detection and suppression strategies historically assumed that extinguishing the visible hot flame eliminated combustion hazards. PSI-117 proves that cool flames can persist undetected in microgravity, releasing flammable fuel vapors and toxic partial oxidation intermediates (aldehydes, carbon monoxide) while burning invisibly.
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)

text:
- **Convective Re-ignition Hazard:** An established cool flame subjected to an increase in cabin ventilation or local draft (e.g., when opening a hatch or turning on an air circulation fan) can undergo rapid kinetic transition back into a vigorous, high-temperature hot flame (flashover / re-ignition).
- **Suppression Envelope Definition:** Conventional inerting strategies must account for the lower temperature and distinct scalar dissipation boundaries of cool flames to achieve complete chemical and thermal extinction, rather than merely knocking down the luminous hot flame.
title: NASA PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics (ISS FLEX Multi-Physics CFD Analysis)
