title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
---

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Rationale
On Earth (1-g), buoyancy causes diffusion flames to flicker, stretch upward, and establish non-uniform velocity fields that obscure the fundamental mechanisms of soot inception, growth, and radiative extinction. In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station (ISS), the suppression of buoyant convection enables the formation of spherical diffusion flames. Under spherical symmetry, convection is purely radial, flame stretch is controlled, and complex 3-D transport reduces to tractable 1-D mathematical descriptions.
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
The ACME Flame Design investigation was conducted in the 100-liter chamber of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to study the physics of non-premixed gaseous combustion. By manipulating the stoichiometric mixture fraction ($Z_{st}$), burner flow rates, inert diluents ($N_2$, $CO_2$), and ambient pressures, Flame Design explored a novel paradigm: establishing soot-free, highly efficient diffusion flames by controlling flame position and temperature gradients relative to fuel pyrolysis zones.

---

## 3. Core Hypotheses & Experimental Architecture
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
---

## 3. Core Hypotheses & Experimental Architecture

### Hypotheses Tested
1. **Soot-Inception Boundary:** Soot formation requires a spatial region where the local carbon-to-oxygen (C/O) ratio and temperature ($T$) simultaneously exceed critical threshold values, and where the aerodynamic strain rate is sufficiently low to allow precursor residence time.
2. **Critical Extinction Temperature:** Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish via radiative cooling when the peak flame temperature decreases below a critical threshold of **1,130 K**.
3. **Steady-State Spherical Flames:** Long-duration, truly steady-state gaseous spherical diffusion flames can be sustained in microgravity despite significant radiative heat losses.
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
### Burner Configurations & Diagnostics
- **Normal Spherical Diffusion Flames:** Fuel gas injected radially outward through a spherical porous burner into an ambient oxidizer environment ($O_2/N_2$ or $O_2/CO_2$).
- **Inverse Spherical Diffusion Flames:** Oxidizer injected outward from the porous burner into an ambient fuel/diluent atmosphere. In inverse flames, fuel is outside the reaction zone, dramatically altering the high-temperature residence time of pyrolysis intermediates.
- **Fuels Tested:**
  - Ethylene ($C_2H_4$): Highly sooting hydrocarbon fuel used to map soot inception limits and soot volume fractions.
  - Methane ($CH_4$): Baseline soot-free hydrocarbon fuel used to isolate thermal radiation and chemical kinetic extinction.
- **Diagnostics Suite:**
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
- **Diagnostics Suite:**
  - Multi-angle high-resolution color cameras and low-light UV imaging.
  - Broad-band radiometers measuring total radiative heat loss ($W/cm^2$).
  - Photomultiplier tubes (PMT) for OH* and CH* chemiluminescence.
  - Fine-wire high-temperature thermocouples measuring flame and burner surface temperatures.
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Soot Suppression by Flame Design:**
   - Demonstrated that by strategically shifting the stoichiometric mixture fraction $Z_{st}$ and optimizing inert dilution, soot formation can be completely suppressed even in ethylene flames.
   - Proved that placing the reaction zone such that the high-temperature region does not overlap with fuel-rich, low-strain zones eliminates soot precursor formation entirely without requiring premixing.
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
2. **Radiative Extinction Limit & Critical 1,130 K Threshold:**
   - Systematically measured the extinction boundaries of quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames.
   - Confirmed that radiative extinction occurs when radiative emission from $H_2O$ and $CO_2$ drops the peak flame temperature below **1,130 K**, where chain-branching kinetics ($H + O_2 \rightarrow OH + O$) can no longer overcome chain-terminating radical recombination.

3. **Warm Flame Chemistry in Spherical Flames:**
   - Uncovered that during the transition to radiative extinction, spherical diffusion flames exhibit **warm flame chemistry**—a intermediate kinetic regime linking high-temperature hot flames with low-temperature cool flame pathways.
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
4. **Confirmation of Steady-State Existence:**
   - Validated that steady-state gaseous spherical diffusion flames exist in microgravity over extended durations ($>60$ seconds), resolving decades of theoretical controversy regarding whether radiative losses would inevitably cause spherical flames to extinguish.

---
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Implications
The empirical and computational results from PSI-10 / ACME Flame Design provide essential engineering guidelines for spacecraft life support and fire protection:
- **Gaseous Fire Extinction Criteria:** Defines the precise atmospheric diluent concentrations ($N_2$, $CO_2$) and chamber pressures necessary to force accidental spacecraft gaseous leaks (e.g., fuel lines, battery offgassing) below the 1,130 K flammability limit.
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

text:
- **Soot-Free Cabin Hazard Control:** Spacecraft smoke detectors rely on optical or ionization detection of soot particles. In low-strain microgravity diffusion flames where soot inception is suppressed or altered, flames can burn cleanly without generating typical soot signatures, posing an invisible thermal threat that standard optical detectors may miss.
- **Radiative Feedback Modeling:** Provides verified radiative heat loss fractions for enclosed microgravity compartments, improving the predictive accuracy of spacecraft fire spread simulations (e.g., Saffire and exploration habitat fire models).
title: NASA PSI-10: ACME Flame Design - Clean Efficient Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity

title: NASA PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity (BASS Validation)

text:
## 2. Scientific Background & The Concurrent Flame Spread Challenge
In spacecraft fire safety, flame spread over solid combustible materials is categorized into two fundamental modes:
1. **Opposed-Flow Flame Spread:** The flame propagates against the direction of the oxidizer flow into cold virgin fuel. In microgravity, opposed flame spread is steady and relatively slow because heat conduction through the gas and solid is limited to a small region upstream of the flame edge.
title: NASA PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity (BASS Validation)

text: 2. **Concurrent-Flow Flame Spread:** The flame propagates in the same direction as the forced oxidizer flow. Here, hot combustion gases, unburned pyrolyzates, and soot are swept forward across the unburned downstream fuel surface. This creates strong convective and radiative thermal feedback, accelerating pyrolysis and causing rapid, potentially catastrophic fire growth.
title: NASA PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity (BASS Validation)

text:
Concurrent flame spread represents one of the most difficult challenges in computational combustion because it couples multi-scale gas-phase aerodynamics, finite-rate chemical kinetics, solid-phase polymer degradation/pyrolysis (charring, bubbling, and ablation), and participating media radiation. Previous attempts to model concurrent flame spread relied on empirical correlations or simplified one-step chemistry models that failed to capture intermediate radical species and extinction boundaries.

---
title: NASA PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity (BASS Validation)

text:
## 3. Unsteady Flamelet Generated Manifolds (UFGM) Formulation
To resolve the intricate coupling of concurrent flame spread without the extreme computational cost of direct numerical simulation (DNS), Investigation PSI-62 formulated and implemented an **Unsteady Flamelet Generated Manifold (UFGM)** model:
- **State Space Reduction:** Pre-computes laminar flamelet solutions using detailed chemical mechanisms (capturing radical pools including OH, H, O, and methyl species) and maps them into lower-dimensional manifolds parameterized by mixture fraction ($Z$) and a progress variable ($C$).
title: NASA PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity (BASS Validation)

text:
- **Radiative Flamelet Coupling:** Incorporates volumetric radiative emission and absorption directly into the manifold generation, accounting for non-adiabatic radiative heat loss that governs near-limit extinction.
- **Solid-Fluid Interface Coupling:** Solves the transient 1-D/2-D condensed-phase energy and mass conservation equations for polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) solid degradation, matching surface mass flux and temperature with gas-phase Navier-Stokes boundary layers.

text:
## 4. Capturing the "Goldilocks" Flammability Zone
A key triumph of the UFGM model was successfully reproducing the non-monotonic **"Goldilocks" flammability boundary** originally documented by NASA GRC scientists Sandra Olson and Paul Ferkul during BASS flight testing:
- **Low-Velocity Quenching Regime ($u < 1$ cm/s):** In quiescent or ultra-low forced airflow, the lack of buoyancy produces thick, extended flame zones. The residence time is long, leading to excessive radiative heat loss to the ambient environment. Gas-phase temperatures drop below the flammability threshold, and the flame self-quenches due to radiative cooling.
title: NASA PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity (BASS Validation)

text:
- **The "Goldilocks" Optimum ($u \sim 2$ to $10$ cm/s):** At intermediate, low forced velocities—matching the typical low-speed ventilation present in spacecraft cabins—oxygen transport is adequate to support robust exothermic reaction while residence times remain long enough for intense radiative feedback to the fuel surface. Here, materials exhibit their maximum flammability and burning rates.
- **High-Velocity Blowoff Regime ($u > 20$ cm/s):** As forced ventilation increases, the convective flow time becomes shorter than the chemical reaction time (Damköhler number $Da < 1$). The high aerodynamic strain stretches the flame base, causing convective blowoff extinction.

- **Two-Color Pyrometry from Flight Video:** Utilized multi-spectral imagery recorded by Nikon DSLR cameras during BASS operations in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG).
- **3D Field Reconstruction:** Applied tomographic inversion algorithms to determine 3-D soot volume fractions ($f_v$) and 2-D temperature fields across burning PMMA samples.

text: - **Radiative Heat Flux Mapping:** Directly measured flame-to-fuel radiative heat flux profiles, demonstrating that radiative feedback from microgravity flames accounts for up to 40-60% of total surface heat flux driving solid fuel pyrolysis.

1. **Subgrid-Scale Models for Spacecraft Fire Safety:** The UFGM framework serves as an accurate, computationally efficient subgrid-scale combustion model for Large Eddy Simulation (LES) codes, enabling whole-compartment fire modeling for human exploration architectures (e.g., Lunar Gateway, Mars transit vehicles, commercial space stations).
2. **Exploration Atmosphere Fire Hazards:** Validates material flammability responses under Space Exploration Atmospheres (SEA) with reduced pressures (e.g., 56 kPa / 8.2 psia) and elevated oxygen concentrations (up to 34% $O_2$).

text: 3. **Ventilation Control Strategy:** Highlights that maintaining minimal cabin ventilation ($2-5$ cm/s) for crew comfort inadvertently places materials precisely within the most hazardous "Goldilocks" flammability zone, reinforcing the necessity of strict non-flammable material screening standards.

title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
---

## 2. Scientific Rationale & The 1-g vs. 0-g Soot Discrepancy
In normal Earth gravity (1-g), strong buoyancy-driven natural convection accelerates hot flame gases upward, creating narrow, flickering diffusion flames. The high buoyant flow velocities limit the residence time of fuel molecules and soot precursors to tens of milliseconds, restricting soot inception, surface growth, and agglomeration.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
In the microgravity (0-g) environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS), buoyant acceleration is absent ($g \sim 10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$ g). Gas transport is dictated purely by low-velocity forced flow and molecular diffusion. Under these conditions:
- Fluid residence times increase by a factor of 5 to 10 compared to normal gravity.
- Laminar diffusion flames become significantly longer, broader, and more diffuse.
- Soot particles have prolonged residence in high-temperature, fuel-rich pyrolysis zones, resulting in drastically higher soot volume fractions ($f_v$) and larger primary particle aggregate clusters.
- Peak flame temperatures are lower due to enhanced volumetric radiative heat loss from the dense soot clouds.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
Understanding this 1-g vs. 0-g discrepancy is paramount for spacecraft fire safety, as soot formation directly governs flame luminosity, radiative heat transfer to surrounding equipment, smoke production, and detector activation thresholds.

---

## 3. Experimental Diagnostics: Color-Ratio Pyrometry on SPICE Flight Imagery
The SPICE investigation flew in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) to determine the "smoke point"—the critical fuel mass flow rate at which soot can no longer be completely oxidized within the flame envelope and escapes into the surrounding environment as unburned carbonaceous smoke.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
Investigation PSI-60 extracted and processed over **1,600 raw 14-bit Nikon NEF digital single-lens reflex (DSLR)** flight images captured during SPICE operations:
- **Multi-Channel Separation:** Decoded raw Bayer matrix images into red, green, and blue spectral channels without lossy compression.
- **Two-Color / Color-Ratio Pyrometry:** Calculated pixel-by-pixel ratios of radiant emission between color channels to reconstruct two-dimensional soot temperature distributions ($T_{soot}$).
- **Absolute Intensity Calibration:** Applied ground-calibrated tungsten ribbon lamp transfer functions to compute absolute line-of-sight soot volume fractions ($f_v$), mapping soot concentrations from the flame base to the open soot-escape tip.

---
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
## 4. Advanced Computational Soot & Radiation Modeling
To simulate the physics observed in the SPICE images, the Yale research team implemented a comprehensive, multi-dimensional numerical reacting flow solver:
- **Coupled Aerodynamics & Chemistry:** Solved the 2-D axisymmetric variable-density Navier-Stokes equations coupled with detailed multi-component gas-phase chemical mechanisms for methane ($CH_4$) and ethylene ($C_2H_4$) fuels.
- **Discrete-Sectional Soot Dynamics:** Integrated a sectional soot model tracking polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) inception, particle coagulation, heterogeneous surface growth via the H-abstraction-$C_2H_2$-addition (HACA) mechanism, particle aggregation, and oxidation by $OH$ and $O_2$.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
- **Volumetric Radiation Re-Absorption:** Unlike conventional optically thin radiation models, PSI-60 implemented a participating media radiation solver accounting for radiation re-absorption by $CO_2$, $H_2O$, and soot particles. In microgravity, up to **15% to 25%** of emitted radiant energy is re-absorbed by cooler incoming reactants and the surrounding gas blanket, significantly altering flame stand-off distances and stability.
- **Burner Architectures Simulated:** Validated across both the Yale coflow burner and the ISS ACME flight burner.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)
NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
## 5. Major Discoveries & Technical Data
1. **Dramatic Elevation of Soot Volume Fractions in Microgravity:**
   - Soot volume fractions in 0-g flames are **2x to 4x higher** than in identical normal-gravity flames at identical fuel and oxidizer flow rates.
2. **Lower Smoke Point in Microgravity:**
   - The fuel flow rate required to cause smoke emission (the smoke point) is markedly lower in microgravity. Flames that are cleanly soot-oxidizing on Earth release heavy streams of smoke and unburned carbonaceous particulates in microgravity.
3. **Suppression of Soot Oxidation at Flame Tips:**
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
3. **Suppression of Soot Oxidation at Flame Tips:**
   - In 1-g, buoyant air entrainment forces oxygen into the flame tip, ensuring complete oxidation. In microgravity, the slow diffusion of oxygen and intense radiative heat loss from the dense soot cloud lower the tip temperature below the threshold for soot oxidation ($\sim 1,300$ K), causing the flame tip to open and emit soot aggregates.
4. **Thermal Feedback Modification via Radiation Re-Absorption:**
   - Soot radiation re-absorption preheats incoming fuel and oxidizer streams, stabilizing the flame base at flow rates where optically thin models incorrectly predict extinction.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)
NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
## 6. Spacecraft Fire Safety & Exploration Engineering Implications
- **Spacecraft Smoke Detector Optimization:** Terrestrial ionization and optical obscuration detectors are engineered for the small soot agglomerates and lower soot yields characteristic of buoyant 1-g fires. PSI-60 proves that in microgravity, even small incipient fires produce large, high-mass-fraction soot agglomerates. Fire detection algorithms must be tuned to microgravity soot size distributions to avoid nuisance alarms while providing early detection of slow-burning electrical or gaseous fires.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

text:
- **Emergency Air Revitalization & Post-Fire Filter Sizing:** The discovery that microgravity flames emit soot at substantially lower fuel flow rates dictates larger particulate capacity requirements for spacecraft Emergency Mask Systems (EMS) and Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) HEPA/charcoal filtration banks.
- **Radiative Hazard Modeling:** Proves that fire safety simulations for exploration habitats (Lunar Gateway, Mars transit) must include radiation re-absorption; ignoring this effect underestimates flame heat transfer to adjacent spacecraft structural components by up to 25%.
title: NASA PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets (Soot Formation in 0g vs 1g)

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Metal Joining Rationale
Long-duration human spaceflight architectures—including the Artemis lunar exploration missions, the Lunar Gateway, and crewed Mars transit vehicles—require robust in-space manufacturing, maintenance, and repair capabilities. In-space soldering and electrical metal joining are essential for servicing mission-critical avionics, communications instrumentation, life support power buses, and science payloads.
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text: However, metal solidification behavior is profoundly altered by the space environment. In terrestrial (1-g) soldering, buoyant natural convection drives gas bubbles and volatilized flux out of the molten pool, yielding dense, low-porosity electrical connections. In microgravity (0-g), buoyant forces are eliminated, fundamentally changing bubble dynamics, heat dissipation, and microstructural development.
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
Investigation PSI-181 analyzed flight hardware from NASA's **In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI)** processed aboard the International Space Station, comparing it against terrestrial controls to quantify how suppressed buoyancy affects internal void formation, thermocapillary Marangoni convection, and electrical/mechanical joint reliability across extreme spaceflight thermal ranges (–157°C to +121°C).

---

## 3. Alloys Evaluated & Experimental Methodology
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
---

## 3. Alloys Evaluated & Experimental Methodology

### Alloy Compositions Tested
1. **ISSI Flight Baseline Alloy:** 40wt% Pb – 60wt% Sn (eutectic lead-tin formulation utilized in flight repairs).
2. **Off-Eutectic Formulation:** 50wt% Pb – 50wt% Sn.
3. **High-Reliability Lead-Free Alloy:** 95.5wt% Sn – 3.8wt% Ag – 0.7wt% Cu (SAC387 alloy evaluated for RoHS/environmental compliance in aerospace electronics).
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
### Multiscale Diagnostics
- **3D Micro-Computed Tomography ($\mu$-CT):** High-resolution X-ray volumetric scanning to image, quantify, and map internal void distributions, pore geometry, and total volumetric porosity.
- **Microstructural & Phase Analysis:** Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS), and Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) to analyze dendritic spacing, intermetallic compound (IMC) formation at copper substrates ($Cu_6Sn_5$ and $Cu_3Sn$), and solute segregation.
- **Micromechanical & Nanoindentation Testing:** In-situ testing spanning extreme thermal regimes from –157°C (deep-space shadow) to +121°C (unshielded solar illumination).
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text: - **Cryogenic Phase Transformation:** Investigated the $\beta$-Sn (tetragonal metallic white tin) to $\alpha$-Sn (diamond cubic brittle gray tin) allotropic phase transition occurring below 13°C ("tin pest"), examining internal stress evolution, volume expansion (~27%), and cryogenic embrittlement.
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Findings & Physical Mechanisms
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
1. **Suppression of Buoyant Gas Escape & Void Entrapment:**
   - In 1-g, buoyant velocity forces volatile flux bubbles to rise and rupture at the free surface.
   - In microgravity, the absence of buoyancy traps volatile bubbles and shrinkage pores inside the solidified joint. Microgravity solder specimens exhibited **substantially higher internal void fractions** compared to terrestrial baselines.
2. **Void-Induced Marangoni Convection:**
   - Surface tension gradients ($\partial \gamma / \partial T$) along the interfaces of entrapped gas bubbles generated localized thermocapillary (Marangoni) convection within the molten liquidus pool. This convective circulation altered local dendritic arm spacing and drove asymmetric solute partitioning before final solidification.
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
3. **Thermal & Mechanical Degradation Across Extreme Thermal Cycling:**
   - Under cyclic thermal loading between –157°C and +121°C, large entrapped voids acted as stress concentrators, promoting micro-crack initiation during thermal expansion mismatches between the solder alloy and copper conductors.
   - Nanoindentation revealed significant degradation in creep resistance and shear strength in microgravity-processed specimens compared to terrestrial controls.
4. **Gravity-Level-Specific Protocols (GLSPs):**
   - Developed standardized procedural protocols for manual and automated soldering, brazing, and metal joining in microgravity and lunar (1/6-g) gravity fields, specifying feed rates, dwell times, and heat sinking geometries to minimize bubble entrapment.
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)
NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
## 5. Direct Spacecraft Fire Safety & Ignition Prevention Ramifications
The findings of PSI-181 have direct relevance to spacecraft fire safety architecture:
- **Electrical Ignition Source Mitigation (NASA-STD-4003):** Electrical arcing and short-circuits represent the primary ignition hazard aboard oxygen-rich crewed spacecraft (as demonstrated in the Apollo 1 spacecraft fire caused by wire arcing, and Apollo 13 tank heater wiring combustion).
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

text:
- **Joule Heating Hot Spots:** Internal voids within microgravity solder joints severely restrict effective electrical cross-sectional area, creating localized regions of elevated electrical resistance. Under high-current power distribution buses, these voids generate severe Joule heating hot-spots capable of exceeding adjacent material pyrolysis temperatures ($>250-300^\circ\text{C}$).
- **Arcing & Insulation Breakdown:** Thermally degraded or mechanically cracked solder joints subject to thermal fatigue and launch/boost vibrations can undergo intermittent contact separation, initiating high-energy electrical arcs that ignite nearby combustible wiring bundles, conformal coatings, or spacecraft payloads in enclosed cabin environments.
title: NASA PSI-181: Solder Joint Performance in Microgravity and Extreme Spacecraft Temperatures (ISSI Investigation)

title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text:

## 2. Research Overview & Microgravity Combustion Rationale
During the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) conducted inside the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS), researchers observed that hydrocarbon fuel droplets did not burn to completion or simply extinguish when their luminous hot flame disappeared. Instead, after visible flame extinction driven by radiative heat loss, the fuel droplet continued to vaporize and burn in a sustained, low-temperature "cool flame" regime ($T \sim 600-900$ K).
title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text:
Investigation PSI-142 was funded under NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system to analyze the archived ISS FLEX flight data and extend the microgravity droplet results to a general 1-D counterflow flame configuration. By combining high-pressure numerical continuation modeling with ozone-sensitized counterflow experiments, the Princeton research team investigated the transition boundaries between hot flames, intermediate-temperature **warm flames**, and low-temperature **cool flames** under combined radiative heat loss and aerodynamic flow stretch.

---

## 3. Major Scientific Discoveries & Physical Mechanisms
title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text:
### 1. Discovery of the "Warm Flame" Regime & Double Reaction Zone
Between classical high-temperature hot flames ($T > 1,400$ K) and low-temperature cool flames ($T \sim 600-900$ K), the investigation uncovered a distinct, multi-stage combustion regime termed **warm flames** ($T \sim 900-1,400$ K):
- **Double Reaction Zone Structure:** Warm diffusion flames exhibit two spatially separated, chemically coupled reaction zones:
  - Zone 1 (Low-temperature radical inception zone): Governed by low-temperature alkylperoxy ($RO_2$) chemistry and isomerization ($QOOH$).
  - Zone 2 (Intermediate-temperature heat release zone): Driven by hydrogen peroxide production and decomposition ($H_2O_2 (+ M) \rightarrow 2OH (+ M)$).
title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text: - **The Kinetic Bridge:** Warm flames serve as the indispensable thermodynamic and kinetic bridge governing transitions between hot and cool flames. Under specific stretch rates, a cooling hot flame does not quench directly to frozen reactants, but transitions into a warm flame, which subsequently stabilizes or evolves into a pure cool flame.
title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text:
### 2. Unified Flammability Limit Diagram
PSI-142 constructed a comprehensive flammability map integrating:
- Hot flame blowoff and radiative extinction boundaries.
- Cool flame stretch extinction and radiation extinction limits.
- Warm flame persistence envelopes across varying oxidizer flow velocities, inert dilutions ($N_2$, $CO_2$), and ambient oxygen concentrations.
title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text:
### 3. Elevated Pressure Flammability Expansion (up to 20–40 atm)
- At normal atmospheric pressure (1 atm), the cool flame flammability region is narrow and highly sensitive to heat loss.
- As ambient pressure increases to 20–40 atm (relevant to advanced propulsion, high-pressure industrial combustors, and closed life-support tanks), low- and intermediate-temperature reaction rates accelerate exponentially.
- This creates an enormous expansion in the flammability envelope of cool and warm flames, enabling stable burning at oxygen concentrations and stretch rates where hot flames cannot exist.

---
title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text:

- **Comprehensive Data Archive:** `PSI-142_Analyzed Data_PSI data summary Princeton with links.xlsx` (735 KB) containing experimental extinction strain rates, radical intermediate concentration measurements ($HO_2$, $H_2O_2$), and numerical continuation solutions.

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety & Hazard Mitigation Implications
The findings from PSI-142 provide vital design and operational criteria for human space exploration:
- **The Invisible Smoldering/Cool Flame Threat:** In microgravity cabins, where buoyant convective cooling is absent, local residence times are long enough for warm and cool diffusion flames to persist undetected. These flames produce little or no visible light and modest thermal signatures, but continuously consume oxygen and generate toxic, flammable partial oxidation intermediates (formaldehyde, carbon monoxide, organic peroxides).
title: NASA PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction (FLEX Extension)

text:
- **Flashover & Re-Ignition Hazards:** If a crew member activates ventilation, opens an access hatch, or alters cabin pressure, the sudden change in scalar dissipation can shift a surviving warm or cool flame back across the transition boundary into a vigorous, high-temperature hot flame (flashover).
- **Suppression Agent Efficacy:** Conventional fire suppressants designed to quench hot flames by lowering flame temperatures below ~1,400 K can leave cool and warm flame chemistry active. Complete spacecraft fire suppression requires sufficient inerting agent concentration to quench intermediate $H_2O_2$ decomposition and low-temperature $RO_2$ radical branching.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Smoke Physics Rationale
Rapid, reliable detection of incipient fires is paramount for crew survival aboard human exploration spacecraft. Aboard pressurized spacecraft, fires can originate from electrical overloads, wiring harness chafing, component overheating, or material smoldering.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
However, the physical properties of smoke emitted by pyrolyzing materials are fundamentally altered by the gravitational environment:
- **Normal Gravity (1-g):** Strong buoyancy-induced natural convection accelerates hot smoke plumes upward away from the pyrolysis zone within tens of milliseconds. This rapid dilution and brief residence time restrict particle coagulation, producing relatively small primary smoke particles and agglomerates (typically 0.05 to 0.3 μm in diameter).
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
- **Microgravity (0-g):** In the absence of buoyancy, gas velocities are governed solely by low-speed cabin ventilation (0.05 to 0.2 m/s) and molecular diffusion. High vapor concentrations linger near the heated material, providing extended residence times that promote continuous vapor condensation, heterogeneous nucleation, and particle-particle Brownian coagulation.
- **The Operational Hazard:** Conventional terrestrial smoke detectors (especially ionization detectors calibrated for small buoyant soot particles) exhibit severe sensitivity degradation when exposed to microgravity smoke, leading to prolonged detection delays or complete failure to alarm during incipient smoldering fires.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 3. Flight Architecture & The SAME-R Investigation
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R, also designated SAME-2) was flown aboard the International Space Station to establish an authoritative, quantitative empirical database of microgravity smoke particulate distributions.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
SAME-R conducted **66 flight test points** between July 16 and September 9, 2010, utilizing the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG). The hardware pyrolyzed five spacecraft-relevant engineering materials under precisely controlled thermal and flow conditions:
1. **Kapton (Polyimide):** Primary high-temperature wiring insulation used throughout aerospace avionics.
2. **Teflon (PTFE):** Fluoropolymer wire insulation and fluid line seal material.
3. **Silicone Rubber:** Aerospace potting compounds, thermal interface pads, and hatch pressure gaskets.
4. **Pyrell® Foam:** Intumescent, fire-retardant open-cell polyurethane foam manufactured by Foamex (introduced in SAME-R to evaluate modern fire-retarded materials).
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text: 5. **Cotton Lamp Wick:** Standard cellulosic smoldering baseline for cross-platform calibration.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
### In-Flight Diagnostics
- **Differential Mobility / Moment-Method Aerosol Sizer:** Utilized unipolar corona aerosol charging and tandem electrometers to determine the first three moments of the particle size distribution in real time.
- **Optical Scattering & Ionization Sensors:** Flown side-by-side with commercial DustTrak photometers and ionization chambers to record real-time detector response curves.
- **Multi-Point Aerosol Sampler (M-pass):** NASA GRC custom collector that deposited smoke particulates onto transmission electron microscopy (TEM) grid substrates for post-flight terrestrial morphology analysis.

---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Massive Particle Size Expansion in Microgravity:**
   - Microgravity smoke particles across all materials exhibited **significantly larger mean diameters** (typically a factor of 2x to 5x larger) and lower particle number densities compared to normal-gravity counterparts produced from identical material masses.
   - Liquid aerosol smokes (particularly silicone and plasticizer pyrolysis) produced large spherical liquid droplets exceeding 1.0 μm, whereas solid polymer pyrolysis (Kapton, Teflon) produced highly branched, fractal-like agglomerates.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Failure Modes of Conventional Spacecraft Smoke Detectors:**
   - **Ionization Detectors:** Sensitivity is roughly proportional to particle diameter ($d_p$). Because microgravity smoke coagulates into fewer, larger particles, the chamber ion capture rate drops dramatically. Ionization detectors exhibited severe alarm delays or failed to alarm even when large smoke masses were generated.
   - **Optical Obscuration Detectors:** Sensitivity is proportional to the projected surface area ($d_p^2$) or scattering cross-section ($d_p^6$ in Rayleigh regime, transitioning to $d_p^2$ in Mie regime). Optical detectors responded more robustly than ionization detectors to large microgravity agglomerates, but suffered from significant calibration shifts between soot types.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
3. **Validation of the Lognormal Moment Method:**
   - Post-flight terrestrial shock-tube and flow-loop calibrations confirmed that microgravity aerosol size distributions follow a lognormal probability density function, enabling high-accuracy reconstruction of particle size and volume fraction from moment measurements.

---
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications
The findings of PSI-101 / SAME-R directly transformed NASA spacecraft design standards:
- **Multi-Criteria Fire Detection Architectures:** Confirmed that single-sensor detectors are fundamentally inadequate for spaceflight. Prompted the development of multi-angle optical scattering detectors coupled with gas-phase chemical sensors (monitoring carbon monoxide CO, carbon dioxide CO$_2$, and acid gases like HF and HCN) for the Orion Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle (MPCV), the Lunar Gateway, and Commercial Crew capsules.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
- **ECLSS Emergency Filter Sizing:** Provided quantitative particulate mass and size distributions necessary to engineer Emergency Mask Systems (EMS) and Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) smoke removal filters capable of capturing large agglomerates without rapid filter face plugging.
- **NASA-STD-6001 Calibration:** Established the empirical baseline required by the NASA Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program to evaluate candidate flight detectors under realistic microgravity aerosol loads.
title: NASA PSI-101: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment - Reflight (SAME-R / SAME-2 ISS Flight Investigation)

## 1. Investigation Team & Institutional Roles

- Co-Investigator (Co-I): Dr. Yasuhiro Kamotani (Case Western Reserve University)

## 2. Executive Summary & Fluid Physics Rationale
In normal Earth gravity (1-g), thermal buoyancy natural convection dominates fluid transport whenever temperature differentials are present. Hot, buoyant fluid rises while cold fluid sinks, largely masking weaker surface-tension-driven flows.
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
In the microgravity environment of spaceflight ($g \le 10^{-5}$ g), buoyant body forces become negligible. When a fluid possesses an unconfined interface or free surface (such as a liquid propellant pool, a burning droplet, an open fluid loop, or a molten solder pool), temperature variations create surface tension gradients along the interface:
$$\frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial T} < 0$$
Because surface tension decreases as temperature rises, fluid is pulled along the interface from warm regions of low surface tension toward cooler regions of high surface tension. Through viscous traction, this interface motion drags bulk fluid beneath it, setting up large-scale convective circulation cells known as **thermocapillary flow** or **Marangoni convection**.
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
The Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1) was a landmark spaceflight investigation flown aboard Space Shuttle Columbia on the STS-50 / USML-1 mission. It provided the world's first comprehensive, high-resolution quantitative dataset of steady and oscillatory thermocapillary convection in microgravity free of buoyant interference.

---
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
## 3. Flight Experimental Architecture & Diagnostics (STS-50 / USML-1)
STDCE-1 was installed inside a dedicated rack within the Spacelab pressurized module aboard STS-50:
- **Test Fluid:** 10 cSt silicone oil (polydimethylsiloxane), selected for its high Prandtl number ($Pr \sim 100$), well-characterized thermophysical properties, non-volatility, and chemical cleanliness.
- **Surface Containment:** Implemented specialized fluoropolymer barrier coatings (3M FC-723) along container rim boundaries to prevent low-surface-tension silicone fluid from creeping or crawling out of the open test cells in microgravity.
- **Two Distinct Heating Modes:**
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
- **Two Distinct Heating Modes:**
  1. *Constant-Flux Laser Heating:* A 10.6 μm $CO_2$ infrared laser beam was directed onto the free surface center, simulating radiant and localized heat deposition.
  2. *Constant-Temperature Cartridge Heating:* A central submerged cylindrical cartridge heater maintained at fixed temperatures, simulating core heating.
- **Diagnostics & Data Collection:**
  - *Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV):* 2-D flow visualization using a continuous laser light sheet illuminating suspended alumina tracer particles, recorded by multi-angle cameras to quantify full velocity vector fields ($u_r, u_z$).
  - *Calibrated Infrared Thermography:* An infrared imaging system focused on the liquid surface provided non-intrusive 2-D temperature distributions ($T(r, \theta)$).
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text: - *Laser Surface Deflection:* Monitored sub-micron free surface deformations and capillary wave oscillations.
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Governing Parameters
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
1. **Governing Dimensionless Scaling Groups:**
   - Identified and experimentally validated the dimensionless parameters controlling microgravity thermocapillary flows:
     - **Marangoni Number:** $Ma = \frac{-(\partial \gamma / \partial T) \Delta T L}{\mu \alpha}$ (ratio of surface-tension forces to viscous-thermal dissipation).
     - **Prandtl Number:** $Pr = \frac{\nu}{\alpha}$ (ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity).
     - **Aspect Ratio:** $Ar = \frac{H}{R}$ (liquid depth to container radius).
     - **Surface Deformation Parameter:** $S = \frac{-(\partial \gamma / \partial T) \Delta T}{\gamma}$ (measure of capillary boundary deformation).
2. **Steady Boundary Layer Scaling:**
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Steady Boundary Layer Scaling:**
   - Confirmed that under steady axisymmetric flow, strong thermocapillary boundary layers form adjacent to the free surface, with boundary layer thickness scaling with $Ma^{-1/3}$.
3. **Onset of Hydrothermal Oscillations:**
   - Discovered that when the temperature gradient exceeds a critical Marangoni number ($Ma_{cr}$), the steady toroidal circulation cell loses stability, transitioning abruptly into an **oscillatory flow regime** characterized by traveling hydrothermal waves, periodic velocity fluctuations, and fluctuating surface temperature patterns.
4. **Coupling with Free Surface Deformations:**
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
4. **Coupling with Free Surface Deformations:**
   - Proved that minute free-surface deformations play an essential role in triggering flow oscillations, refuting earlier rigid-lid numerical models that failed to predict the onset of instability.
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)
NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
## 5. Direct Cross-Disciplinary Relevance to Spacecraft Fire Safety & Materials Processing
While classified under Fluid Physics, the fundamental findings of STDCE-1 directly govern several critical microgravity combustion and spacecraft safety phenomena:
- **Flame Spread Across Liquid Fuels:** In microgravity pool fires, flame propagation is governed by thermocapillary Marangoni convection ahead of the flame front. Hot combustion gases heat the fuel surface, driving liquid fuel forward along the surface toward cooler fuel, which preheats downstream reactants and dictates whether the flame spreads steadily or exhibits pulsating behavior.
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

text:
- **Liquid Droplet Internal Circulation:** In droplet combustion (such as FLEX on the ISS), surface tension gradients along the droplet exterior induce internal Marangoni circulation cells that govern liquid-phase species transport and preferential vaporization.
- **In-Space Solder and Metal Joining Integrity (PSI-181):** In microgravity brazing, welding, and soldering, void-induced Marangoni convection around trapped gas bubbles drives solute segregation, asymmetric dendritic growth, and mechanical porosity.
- **Cryogenic Propellant Management:** Governs bubble migration, thermal destratification, and phase change in Zero-Boil-Off (ZBO) cryogenic oxygen and methane propellant tanks for deep-space exploration craft.
title: NASA PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 (STDCE-1 Space Shuttle Flight Investigation)

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Smoke Physics Rationale
The primary goal of the PSI-115 investigation was to apply advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) to analyze the fundamental fluid mechanical and aerosol dynamic mechanisms governing smoke generation, nucleation, agglomeration, and transport in reduced gravity.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text: Aboard human spacecraft such as the International Space Station (ISS), the Orion spacecraft, and future lunar/Martian transit habitats, early fire detection is the primary defense against catastrophic loss of life and vehicle. However, smoke aerosol generation in microgravity deviates substantially from terrestrial behavior due to the complete absence of buoyancy-driven natural convection:
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text: - **Terrestrial Normal Gravity (1g):** Thermal expansion generates strong buoyant upward plumes ($Gr/Re^2 \gg 1$) that accelerate hot pyrolysis vapors away from heated elements within tens of milliseconds. This rapid advective displacement imposes steep dilution gradients, limiting the local precursor concentration and producing brief residence times that yield smaller primary aerosol particulates (typically 0.05 to 0.3 μm in diameter).
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text: - **Microgravity (0g):** In the absence of buoyant acceleration ($Gr \to 0$), fluid motion is dictated entirely by molecular diffusion and forced low-velocity ventilation (typically 0.05 to 0.2 m/s). Pyrolysis vapor stagnates near the overheated material, creating high vapor concentrations and extended residence times in elevated temperature zones. These conditions dramatically enhance supersaturation, homogeneous nucleation, and Brownian coagulation, generating smoke particles that are significantly larger in mean diameter and lower in number density.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text: - **Detector Vulnerabilities:** Terrestrial ionization smoke detectors calibrated for small, high-mobility soot particles exhibit critical sensitivity degradation or failure when exposed to large microgravity smoke agglomerates, creating dangerous alarm latency.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:

PSI-115 utilized high-order, fully resolved Direct Numerical Simulation based on a nodal Navier-Stokes formulation coupled with aerosol population balance equations:

text: where $\mathbf{g} = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$ for 1g simulations and $\mathbf{g} = 0$ for microgravity simulations.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:
2. **Aerosol Dynamic Model:**
   The investigation modeled the formation, nucleation, growth, and transport of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) aerosol droplets—the primary surrogate fluid used during the NASA Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) calibrations:
   - **Homogeneous Nucleation:** Governed by classical nucleation theory based on local vapor supersaturation ratio $S = P_v / P_{sat}(T)$.
   - **Vapor Condensation / Evaporation:** Driven by the vapor concentration gradient between the particle surface and surrounding bulk gas.
   - **Brownian Coagulation:** Evaluated using the Fuchs-Sutugin transition-regime kernel covering both free-molecular ($Kn \gg 1$) and continuum ($Kn \ll 1$) regimes.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:
- **Thermophoretic Transport:** Particle drift velocities induced by strong thermal gradients:
     $$\mathbf{u}_{th} = -K_{th} \frac{\nu}{T} \nabla T$$
     which drive aerosol particles away from hot heated surfaces toward cooler ambient gas.
   - **Gravitational Settling:** Included in 1g baselines and neglected in 0g conditions.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:
3. **Flow Geometry & Boundary Conditions:**
   Simulations replicated the exact flow channel geometry of the NASA SAME and SAME-R flight experiments:
   - Heated sample surface expelling pyrolysis vapor into a rectangular duct.
   - Cross-flow speeds evaluated at low velocities, including 8 cm/s ($0.08\ \text{m/s}$), where the Richardson number ($Ri = Gr/Re^2$) is large in 1g, ensuring clear comparison between buoyancy-dominated and diffusion-dominated regimes.

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Insights
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Insights

1. **Wake Structure Transformation (Buoyant vs Non-Buoyant):**
   - At 8 cm/s cross-flow in normal gravity (1g), thermal buoyancy creates a powerful asymmetric updraft with intense vortex shedding behind the heated sample. The wake tilts upward, rapidly venting vapor away from the surface into the upper boundary layer.
   - In microgravity (0g), the wake remains straight, symmetric, and laminar. Thermal and species boundary layers thicken smoothly along the downstream coordinate.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:
2. **Supersaturation Fields & Nucleation Rates:**
   - In 1g, buoyant dilution disperses the vapor concentration field rapidly, restricting high supersaturation ($S > 1$) to a narrow thin layer above the heating element. Nucleation is brief and spatially confined.
   - In 0g, the absence of buoyant uplift maintains high vapor mass fractions over an extended downstream distance. Consequently, the nucleation rate remains active over a spatial volume more than an order of magnitude larger than in 1g, resulting in substantial total particle production.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:
3. **Particle Size Distribution (PSD) Evolution:**
   - DNS resolved instantaneous and time-averaged scalar fields of particle number density ($N$), mean particle diameter ($d_p$), and total smoke volume fraction.
   - Microgravity conditions yielded a Particle Size Distribution shifted strongly toward larger particle modes due to prolonged residence time inside the high-concentration vapor plume, allowing Brownian agglomeration and condensation to dominate.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:
4. **Thermophoretic Deposition vs Clearance:**
   - In 1g, buoyant updrafts overpower thermophoretic drift near the heated source.
   - In 0g, thermophoresis creates a distinct particle-free "cushion" directly adjacent to the hot surface, driving newly formed smoke particulates into the cooler outer flow streamlines without any buoyancy-assisted venting.

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety & Life Support Engineering Ramifications

1. **Optimizing Spacecraft Fire Detectors:**
   - Conventional spacecraft fire detection architectures have historically relied on ionization chambers optimized for small terrestrial soot particles ($0.05 - 0.2\ \mu\text{m}$).
   - The DNS results from PSI-115 confirm that microgravity smoke particulates from pyrolyzing polymers and plasticizers rapidly grow into the super-micron regime ($> 0.5 - 2.0\ \mu\text{m}$).
   - These findings reinforce the transition across NASA exploration vehicles (Orion, Gateway, Commercial Crew) to multi-angle optical scatter detectors, which scale with the optical scattering cross section ($\sim d_p^2$ to $d_p^6$) and perform superiorly on large microgravity smoke aerosols.
title: NASA PSI-115: Utilization of SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity

text:
2. **Smoke Transport Modeling in Spacecraft Cabins:**
   - Provides fundamental fluid dynamic benchmark data to calibrate engineering CFD codes (such as NIST Fire Dynamics Simulator - FDS) used to design airflow ventilation and smoke detector placement in spacecraft modules.

3. **ECLSS Smoke Filtration and Scrubbing:**
   - Accurate particle size distributions and number densities are critical to sizing post-fire Emergency Mask Systems (EMS) and Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) HEPA / charcoal scrubbers to prevent premature filter clogging.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Fire Safety Rationale

For over five decades, human spaceflight missions have relied on terrestrial laboratory testing (specifically **NASA-STD-6001 Test 1: Upward Flame Propagation**) to screen and certify materials for flight. In NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, small material samples (approximately $5\ \text{cm} \times 30\ \text{cm}$) are mounted vertically in normal gravity (1g) and ignited at the bottom in an upward buoyant airflow. If the flame self-extinguishes before burning 15 cm of the sample, the material passes and is rated non-flammable.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
However, the international combustion science community recognized severe, unquantified risks in this methodology:
1. **Buoyancy Decoupling:** In normal gravity, natural convection pulls hot combustion products upward at $1.0 - 2.0\ \text{m/s}$, inducing massive entrainment that cools the burning base while simultaneously accelerating upward spread. In microgravity (0g), buoyant flow drops to zero; gas motion is controlled strictly by gentle forced cabin ventilation ($0.05 - 0.2\ \text{m/s}$) and molecular diffusion.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text: 2. **The Scale Problem:** Due to strict safety constraints, microgravity combustion experiments aboard crewed spacecraft (Space Shuttle, Mir, ISS) were restricted to small samples (typically $< 10\ \text{cm}$ in dimension). Small samples have high edge heat losses and small flame volumes, causing them to extinguish easily. Real fires, however, grow into large structures where flame-to-fuel radiative preheating scales dramatically with fuel surface area ($\propto L^2$).
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text: 3. **The Saffire Solution:** To bridge this critical knowledge gap without risking astronaut safety, NASA developed the **Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire)** series, conducting large-scale, deliberate fire experiments inside an uncrewed commercial cargo resupply vehicle (Orbital ATK Cygnus) after it completes its ISS delivery mission and unberths to enter free flight before atmospheric re-entry.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
---

## 3. Flight Architecture & The SAFFIRE-I Experiment
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
Saffire-I executed the **largest controlled fire ever ignited in space**:
- **Flight Platform:** Orbital ATK Cygnus CRS OA-6 (SS Rick Husband) cargo capsule after de-berthing from the ISS Harmony module.
- **Enclosure:** A self-contained flow duct measuring $0.9\ \text{m} \times 0.5\ \text{m} \times 1.4\ \text{m}$, installed in the pressurized cargo bay of the Cygnus vehicle.
- **Test Sample:** A solid composite fabric known as **Sibal**:
  - Composition: 75% cotton, 25% fiberglass blend by weight.
  - Dimensions: **0.94 meters long by 0.40 meters wide** ($94\ \text{cm} \times 40\ \text{cm}$).
  - Areal Density: Nominally $18\ \text{mg/cm}^2$.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
- Areal Density: Nominally $18\ \text{mg/cm}^2$.
  - Rationale: The cotton fibers provide a realistic cellulosic biomass combustion source, while the inert woven fiberglass substrate maintains dimensional integrity after the cotton is pyrolyzed, preventing the burning fabric from curling, tearing, or floating away in the low-gravity flow.
- **Flow & Environmental Conditions:**
  - Ambient atmosphere: Cygnus cabin air (~21% O$_2$, ~79% N$_2$, nominal spacecraft atmospheric pressure ~101 kPa).
  - Flow velocity: A controlled, uniform concurrent forced airflow of **20 cm/s** ($0.2\ \text{m/s}$) blown along the sample surface.
  - Ignition: A continuous Kanthal hot-wire igniter situated along the upstream leading edge of the Sibal fabric, energized to trigger uniform line ignition.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
### High-Fidelity In-Flight Instrumentation
- **Dual Camera Imaging Systems:**
  - Camera Set 1 (S1C1, S1C2): Calibrated high-speed color video tracking the advancing flame front, soot emission, and luminous zone.
  - Camera Set 2 (S2C1, S2C2): Wide-angle and oblique perspective cameras tracking surface pyrolysis, char formation, and trailing edge burnout.
- **Gas Diagnostics:** Non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) and electrochemical sensors monitoring oxygen consumption ($\Delta \text{O}_2$), carbon dioxide generation ($\text{CO}_2$), and carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$).
- **Thermal Diagnostic Rakes:** Multipoint thermocouple arrays recording upstream flow temperature, gas-phase flame temperature, and duct exhaust temperatures.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
- **Radiometers:** Broad-band radiometers measuring radiant heat flux emitted from the flame sheet back to the fuel and duct walls.
- **Flow Sensors:** Differential pressure transducers and hot-wire anemometers verifying uniform duct velocity profiles.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Flame Spread Dynamics & Quasi-Steady Velocity:**
   - Following upstream ignition, the flame grew rapidly across the full 40 cm width and established a continuous, luminous planar flame sheet propagating concurrently with the 20 cm/s flow.
   - The flame front attained a quasi-steady spread rate of **$V_f \approx 0.28 - 0.32\ \text{cm/s}$**, burning stably for over 8 minutes until consuming the cotton content across the entire 0.94-meter length.
   - The steady flame length exceeded 25 cm, demonstrating that microgravity flames over large samples are far larger and more persistent than predicted by small-scale drop-tower or glovebox tests.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
2. **The Scale Effect & Radiative Preheating:**
   - In small-scale microgravity tests, flame spread is often slow and prone to quenching due to radiative and convective heat loss from narrow flame edges.
   - In Saffire-I, the large flame area ($0.4\ \text{m} \times >0.25\ \text{m}$) generated intense radiative feedback that preheated the virgin fuel far downstream of the pyrolysis front. This sustained robust flame propagation in flow regimes where small laboratory samples extinguish.
   - This empirically demonstrated that **small-scale flammability screening (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) is not conservative** for predicting large-scale fire hazards in space habitats.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
3. **Structural Stability of Composite Char:**
   - The fiberglass matrix retained its weave structure throughout the burn, confirming that composite materials can be engineered to prevent catastrophic breakup and airborne ember generation during low-gravity fires.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
4. **Transient Model Validation:**
   - Extensive post-flight modeling by Case Western Reserve University (Li, Liao, and T'ien) validated 2D and 3D transient Navier-Stokes combustion models against Saffire-I experimental data.
   - Numerical predictions of flame front position versus time, pyrolyzed mass loss rate, and oxygen depletion curves achieved extraordinary agreement ($< 8\%$ deviation), confirming that computational combustion models can accurately simulate large-scale spacecraft fires when informed by microgravity transport physics.

---

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text:
The groundbreaking results of Saffire-I directly impacted NASA and international space exploration architectures:
- **Revision of Exploration Atmosphere Flammability Standards:** Validated material flammability for exploration atmospheres planned for the Artemis Program, Lunar Gateway, and Mars transit habitats (e.g., 34% O$_2$ at 8.2 psia / 56.5 kPa, normoxic conditions).
- **Cabin Fire Sensor Positioning:** Demonstrated that low-speed ventilation ($0.1 - 0.2\ \text{m/s}$) creates coherent, non-dispersing smoke and combustion product streams that follow duct streamlines rather than rising to the ceiling, dictating that spacecraft smoke detectors must be positioned directly in return air ducts rather than on cabin ceilings.
title: NASA PSI-98: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I Large-Scale Microgravity Flame Spread)

text: - **Post-Fire Response Protocols:** Provided empirical carbon monoxide and particulate yield data required to size crew emergency breathing apparatus (Emergency Mask Systems) and ECLSS rapid cabin scrubbing procedures.

text:
---

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Cool Flame Physics Rationale
The discovery of spherical, self-sustaining "cool flames" burning in microgravity aboard the International Space Station revolutionized low-temperature hydrocarbon combustion physics. In terrestrial 1g environments, buoyancy-driven natural convection quickly destabilizes and extinguishes low-temperature reaction fronts, making steady observation of isolated droplet cool flames nearly impossible.
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
In the microgravity environment of the ISS, spherically symmetric conditions eliminate buoyant convection, allowing thermal diffusion and molecular transport to balance chemical heat release. The Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) was conceived to fundamentally resolve:
1. The conditions under which liquid hydrocarbon fuels (such as n-dodecane, iso-dodecane blends, and renewable biofuels like farnesane) support self-sustaining, quasi-steady cool flame combustion following hot-flame extinction.
2. The low-temperature chemistry (temperatures between 600 K and 1000 K) dominated by peroxy radical addition ($\text{R} + \text{O}_2 \leftrightarrow \text{RO}_2 \leftrightarrow \text{QOOH} + \text{O}_2 \leftrightarrow \text{OOQOOH}$), chain-branching, and keto-hydroperoxide decomposition.
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
3. The influence of ambient pressure (0.25 atm to 5.0 atm), inert gas composition (nitrogen vs helium dilution), and initial droplet diameter on cool flame extinction limits ($d_{\text{ext}}$).
4. Critical spacecraft fire safety implications: identifying hidden low-temperature smoldering and flameless re-ignition hazards that remain undetectable by visual or thermal sensors in spaceflight cabins.
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)
NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
## 3. Flight Architecture & The CFI Experimental Apparatus
The CFI experiments were conducted within the **Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)** using the **Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)** in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:
- **Combustion Chamber & Gas Delivery:** Hermetically sealed 100-liter chamber with precise gas mixing bottles providing test atmospheres from 0.25 atm up to 5.0 atm, with varying oxygen indices (12% to 30% O$_2$) diluted with nitrogen ($N_2$) or helium ($He$) to probe Lewis number ($Le$) and thermal conduction effects.
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
- **Droplet Dispensing & Deployment:** Syringe-driven dispensing mechanism delivering liquid fuel droplets with initial diameters between $1.5\ \text{mm}$ and $5.0\ \text{mm}$. Droplets were deployed either freely floating or tethered between ultra-fine silicon carbide (SiC, $\sim 14\ \mu\text{m}$) fibers to minimize intrusive conduction heat losses.
- **Tested Fuels:**
  - Pure $n$-dodecane ($n\text{-C}_{12}\text{H}_{26}$): Standard diesel / kerosene surrogate.
  - $n$-dodecane / iso-dodecane binary mixtures: Evaluating branched paraffin octane/cetane rating impacts.
  - Farnesane: Branched renewable bio-derived alkane.
- **Ignition & Diagnostics:**
  - Retractable twin Kanthal hot-wire loops energized to ignite a conventional high-temperature hot flame ($T > 1500\ \text{K}$).
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
- Following hot flame extinction (radiative or diffusive quench), the droplet entered a second-stage, invisible cool flame burning regime.
  - **High-Bitrate Multispectral Camera (HIBMS):** Backlit high-speed monochrome camera recording droplet silhouette shrinkage to measure burning rates (the $d^2$-law: $d^2(t) = d_0^2 - K t$).
  - **Intensified UV / Narrowband Cameras (INTNS):** Capturing ultra-weak chemiluminescence from excited formaldehyde ($\text{H}_2\text{CO}^*$) and hydroxyl radicals ($\text{OH}^*$).
  - **Broadband Radiometers:** Monitoring absolute radiant heat emissions across the ignition, hot-flame burn, transition, and cool-flame extinction phases.
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Insights

1. **Quasi-Steady Cool Flame Burning Regime:**
   - CFI established conclusively that after radiative extinction of the hot flame, droplets of $n$-alkanes continue to vaporize and burn at a quasi-steady rate supported purely by low-temperature cool flame chemistry.
   - The cool flame burning rate constant ($K_{\text{cool}}$) is approximately 2 to 4 times lower than the hot flame burning rate constant ($K_{\text{hot}}$), maintaining steady liquid consumption without visible soot or hot luminosity.
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
2. **Cool Flame Extinction Diameters ($d_{\text{ext}}$):**
   - For a given ambient oxygen concentration and pressure, a distinct critical droplet diameter exists below which the cool flame extinguishes.
   - For $n$-dodecane in air at 1 atm, cool flame extinction occurs at droplet diameters typically between $1.0\ \text{mm}$ and $2.0\ \text{mm}$, governed by a competition between chemical residence time and diffusive scalar dissipation.

3. **Helium Dilution & Lewis Number Effects:**
   - Replacing $N_2$ with helium ($He$) increases gas thermal conductivity and suppresses cool flame stability, elevating the limiting oxygen index required to sustain cool flame burning.
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

4. **Pressure Dependence (0.25 to 5.0 atm):**
   - Higher ambient pressure drastically expands the cool flame burning envelope, accelerating low-temperature alkylperoxy addition pathways and enabling cool flames at lower ambient oxygen concentrations.

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering Ramifications

1. **Ghost Fire / Flameless Re-Ignition Hazards:**
   - In spacecraft cabins, liquid hydrocarbon leaks or polymer pyrolysis products can sustain self-propagating low-temperature cool flame burning that emits negligible visible light or thermal infrared radiation.
   - If cabin ventilation or oxygen partial pressure subsequently shifts, these surviving cool flames can abruptly transition back into intense, high-temperature hot flames (flashover re-ignition).
title: NASA PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
2. **Sensor Calibration for Human Spaceflight:**
   - Conventional spacecraft fire detection relies on visual optical cameras, near-IR thermal detectors, or standard smoke detectors. CFI proved that low-temperature combustion occurs with zero soot formation and negligible IR radiation.
   - Detectors for long-duration exploration habitats (Gateway, Mars transit) must incorporate gas-phase chemical sensors monitoring formaldehyde ($\text{CH}_2\text{O}$), carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$), and unburned fuel vapors to capture incipient cool flame hazards.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Aerosol Physics Rationale
The Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) was the landmark baseline flight investigation conducted aboard the International Space Station to characterize the physical properties, size distributions, and morphology of smoke particulates generated in microgravity.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text: Prior to SAME, spacecraft smoke detection systems (including the ionization smoke detectors aboard the Space Shuttle and early ISS modules) were certified exclusively using terrestrial 1g test fires. However, combustion scientists hypothesized that the physics of smoke generation is fundamentally altered by gravity:
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text: 1. **Hypothesis 1 (Absence of Buoyancy):** In terrestrial 1g fires, intense buoyant natural convection rapidly purges smoke away from pyrolyzing materials at speeds exceeding $1.0\ \text{m/s}$, diluting vapor concentrations and limiting aerosol residence times. In microgravity (0g), buoyant acceleration is absent ($g \approx 0$). Fluid velocities drop to low-speed forced ventilation ($0.05 - 0.2\ \text{m/s}$) and molecular diffusion. Pyrolysis vapors linger near the overheated material, leading to elevated vapor concentrations and prolonged residence times that dramatically amplify homogeneous nucleation, vapor condensation, and Brownian coagulation.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Hypothesis 2 (Super-Micron Aerosol Growth):** Because of this extended residence time in microgravity, liquid aerosol smokes (such as pyrolyzed silicones or plasticizers) and solid polymer smokes will exhibit substantially larger particle diameters ($d_p$) and lower number densities ($N$) than identical smokes generated under 1g conditions.
3. **Hypothesis 3 (Operational Failure of Conventional Detectors):** Conventional ionization detectors, which depend directly on high particle mobility and number density to capture ions, will suffer catastrophic loss of sensitivity or extended alarm delays when exposed to large microgravity smoke agglomerates.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)
NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

## 3. Flight Architecture & The SAME In-Flight Hardware
The SAME investigation operated inside the **Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)** in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:
- **Flow Duct & Material Heating:** A sealed, low-speed flow tunnel with controlled core flow velocities ($0.05$ to $0.2\ \text{m/s}$) delivering filtered cabin air over resistance-heated material samples.
- **Tested Spacecraft Engineering Materials:**
  1. **Kapton (Polyimide):** Primary high-voltage wiring insulation in spacecraft avionics.
  2. **Teflon (PTFE):** Wire cabling jacket and fluid seal polymer.
  3. **Silicone Rubber:** Spacecraft hatch seals, potting compounds, and thermal interface materials.
  4. **Celcon (Polyoxymethylene):** Common engineering thermoplastic.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
4. **Celcon (Polyoxymethylene):** Common engineering thermoplastic.
  5. **Cotton Lamp Wick:** Standard baseline cellulosic smoldering fuel.
- **Real-Time Aerosol Diagnostics:**
  - **Moment-Method Aerosol Sizer:** Utilized unipolar corona aerosol charging coupled with dual-stage electrometers to measure the zeroth ($N$), first ($d_{\text{avg}}$), and second moments of the particle size distribution in real time without bulky terrestrial laboratory spectrometers.
  - **Parallel Detector Test Chamber:** Flown side-by-side with Space Shuttle / ISS flight ionization chambers, commercial ionization sensors, and forward/backward optical scattering photometers.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text: - **Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) Sampler:** Multi-point electrostatic and thermophoretic precipitators capturing smoke particles on carbon-coated TEM copper grids for post-flight morphological analysis on Earth.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Experimental Proof of Microgravity Particle Size Expansion:**
   - SAME flight data proved that microgravity smoke particles across all materials are **consistently 2x to 5x larger in mean diameter** than normal-gravity smoke produced from identical masses and thermal heating rates.
   - Silicone and plasticizer pyrolysis yielded large spherical liquid aerosol droplets exceeding $1.0 - 2.5\ \mu\text{m}$ in diameter, whereas terrestrial 1g baselines remained sub-micron ($0.1 - 0.3\ \mu\text{m}$).
   - Solid polymer pyrolysis (Kapton, Teflon) produced highly branched, fractal-like agglomerates with lower packing densities.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Quantified Failure Modes of Spacecraft Ionization Detectors:**
   - In 1g, ionization detectors alarm quickly because billions of small, high-mobility soot particles efficiently intercept alpha-particle ionization currents.
   - In 0g, the coagulation of smoke into fewer, larger super-micron agglomerates causes a severe drop in the particle number density ($N$). As a result, the ionization chamber current change is minimal, causing extended alarm delays or total failure to alarm during incipient smoldering stages.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
3. **Superior Performance of Optical Scatter Detectors:**
   - Optical scattering cross-sections scale with particle diameter ($d_p^2$ to $d_p^6$). Consequently, optical smoke detectors exhibited significantly enhanced sensitivity to large microgravity smoke aerosols compared to ionization chambers, providing much faster warning times for crew response.
