## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Redesign of Exploration Fire Architecture:**
   - The findings of PSI-102 established the definitive scientific justification for retiring pure ionization smoke detectors from NASA exploration programs.
   - Directly led to the adoption of multi-wavelength, multi-angle optical scattering detectors coupled with carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and acid gas sensors for the Orion Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle (MPCV), Boeing Starliner, SpaceX Dragon, and the Lunar Gateway.
title: NASA PSI-102: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Ventilation Duct Placement Strategy:**
   - Proved that without buoyancy to drive smoke toward the module ceiling, smoke follows forced ventilation streamlines. Consequently, spacecraft fire sensors must be installed directly inside return air ducts and ventilation grilles rather than on cabin bulkheads.

3. **ECLSS Emergency Filter Sizing:**
   - Established the particulate mass loading and size spectrum required to engineer Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) HEPA / charcoal scrubbers and Emergency Mask Systems (EMS) to avoid filter face plugging during post-fire recovery operations.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Diffusion Flame Physics Rationale
Non-premixed laminar diffusion flames form the fundamental physical archetype for burning across power generation, industrial furnaces, and catastrophic fires. On Earth, natural convective buoyancy dominates the flow field around diffusion flames ($Gr \gg 1$), accelerating hot combustion gases upward and inducing strong inward flow strain at the burner rim. This buoyancy-induced strain thins the reaction zone, compresses flame width, and dictates flame liftoff and blowout limits.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, buoyancy is eliminated ($Gr \to 0$). Gas velocities are governed exclusively by low-speed momentum of the fuel jet and forced coflowing air. Under these conditions:
1. **Flame Morphology & Radiative Cooling:** Diffusion flames expand into wide, globular structures with substantially extended residence times. Molecular diffusion dominates fuel-oxidizer transport, and soot particles linger in high-temperature zones, dramatically increasing radiative heat loss.
2. **Liftoff & Stabilization Mechanics:** Without buoyancy-induced shear strain at the burner rim, the flame stabilization zone at the burner base experiences radically different local velocity gradients, altering the liftoff velocity limits and anchor mechanisms.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text: 3. **Soot Formation & Inception:** Soot nucleation, surface growth, and agglomeration pathways are altered by extended residence times and reduced strain rates, presenting critical risks for spacecraft smoke generation and radiative flame spread.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)
NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
## 3. Flight Architecture & The SLICE Apparatus
The SLICE investigation was deployed within the **Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)** in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:
- **Burner Architecture:** Exchangeable stainless-steel fuel tubes of varying internal diameters ($d = 0.8\ \text{mm}$ to $3.0\ \text{mm}$) centered coaxially inside a vertical flow duct.
- **Coflow Air Duct:** Fan-driven flow straighteners and honeycomb flow conditioning supplying uniform, low-velocity laminar coflow air ($u_{\text{air}} \approx 0.05 - 0.4\ \text{m/s}$) surrounding the fuel jet.
- **Fuels Tested:**
  - Pure methane ($\text{CH}_4$) and ethylene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$).
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
- **Fuels Tested:**
  - Pure methane ($\text{CH}_4$) and ethylene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$).
  - Nitrogen-diluted mixtures (e.g., $50\%\ \text{CH}_4 / 50\%\ \text{N}_2$, $30\%\ \text{CH}_4 / 70\%\ \text{N}_2$, and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 / \text{N}_2$ blends) to isolate thermal dilution from chemical kinetics.
- **Diagnostic Systems:**
  - High-resolution digital color camera capturing calibrated still images and high-definition video with synchronized telemetry overlays (mass flow rates, duct temperature, burner pressure).
  - Spectrally filtered chemiluminescence measuring excited hydroxyl ($\text{OH}^*$) and methylidyne ($\text{CH}^*$) radicals marking the heat release zone and flame base anchor location.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text: - Over **4,000 high-resolution images** recorded across 13 major flight test matrices.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Flame Widening & Stabilization Envelope:**
   - In 1g, buoyancy accelerates the hot gas plume upward, producing tall, slender flames that lift off when the fuel jet velocity exceeds the buoyant base stabilization speed.
   - In microgravity (0g), diffusion flames expand radially by a factor of 2x to 3x, forming broad, dome-shaped flame sheets.
   - The absence of buoyant shear strain at the burner rim allows microgravity flames to remain securely anchored at much higher fuel jet velocities than on Earth, significantly expanding the stable burner operating envelope.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Fuel Dilution & Soot Suppression:**
   - Diluting methane and ethylene with molecular nitrogen ($N_2$) reduces peak flame temperatures and delays polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) soot precursors.
   - In 0g, undiluted ethylene flames exhibited heavy soot emissions and intense orange-yellow luminescence. Adding $N_2$ diluent successfully shifted the flame into a clean, soot-free blue reaction regime, mapping the exact dilution thresholds needed to eliminate smoke generation in microgravity.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
3. **Validation of High-Order Flame Codes:**
   - Experimental flame shapes, liftoff heights, and $\text{CH}^*$ chemiluminescence fields provided benchmark validation data for 2D elliptic and boundary-layer Navier-Stokes combustion codes developed by Smooke, Long, and Takahashi.
   - Numerical simulations with detailed chemical kinetics and complex multicomponent molecular diffusion matched measured flame lengths and liftoff heights with exceptional precision ($< 5\%$ error).

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Gas Jet Leaks & Flammability Limits in Spacecraft Cabins:**
   - Spacecraft fluid propulsion systems, life support plumbing, and scientific experiments carry pressurized gaseous fuels (methane, hydrogen, ethylene).
   - SLICE proved that gaseous leaks in microgravity support wider, more stable flames at lower flow speeds than on Earth, meaning small leaks that would blow out or self-extinguish under buoyant drafts in 1g can form stable, persistent fires in microgravity.
title: NASA PSI-106: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE ISS Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Soot & Radiative Heat Flux Hazards:**
   - Radiative heat loss from sooting diffusion flames in 0g accounts for a much larger fraction of total chemical heat release ($\sim 30 - 45\%$) due to large flame surface area and long residence times. This radiant flux can rapidly heat adjacent spacecraft polymers and structural bulkheads to their pyrolysis threshold, causing rapid fire spread across cabin compartments.

3. **CFD Tool Calibration for Vehicle Design:**
   - Provides benchmark microgravity datasets to validate fire modeling tools used by NASA and commercial spaceflight providers to design ventilation airflow, flame arrestors, and emergency gas isolation valves.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Flammability Rationale
While Saffire-I (PSI-98) evaluated a single, massive fabric sample ($0.94\ \text{m} \times 0.40\ \text{m}$) to resolve the scale effect, **Saffire-II (PSI-99)** was specifically architected to evaluate the low-gravity flammability limits and burning kinetics of multiple standard spacecraft materials in direct comparison to NASA's terrestrial material screening standard: **NASA-STD-6001 Test 1**.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 tests small sample strips ($5\ \text{cm} \times 30\ \text{cm}$) in an upward buoyant 1g flow. However:
1. In 1g upward tests, buoyancy forces hot gases up the sample surface, driving rapid convective preheating but also inducing strong air entrainment that cools the pyrolysis base.
2. In microgravity (0g), buoyant acceleration is absent. Gas flow is dictated entirely by gentle forced ventilation ($0.1 - 0.3\ \text{m/s}$), which alters convective heat transfer, expands thermal boundary layers, and eliminates buoyant turbulence.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text: 3. Materials rated "non-flammable" under 1g standard tests can become flammable in microgravity when subjected to low-velocity forced flows, due to the lack of buoyant heat-sink dissipation and enhanced radiative feedback from persistent flames.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
To provide definitive empirical data, Saffire-II tested a **multi-sample card containing nine distinct material samples** under controlled microgravity airflow aboard the uncrewed Cygnus CRS OA-5 vehicle.

---

## 3. Flight Architecture & The SAFFIRE-II Experiment
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
### Flight Hardware & Flow Duct
The Saffire-II hardware was housed inside the pressurized cargo module of the Orbital ATK Cygnus vehicle:
- **Flow Duct:** Transparent polycarbonate duct ($0.9\ \text{m} \times 0.5\ \text{m} \times 1.4\ \text{m}$) equipped with flow straighteners at the inlet and variable-speed suction fans at the exhaust, generating uniform laminar airflow at velocities of **20 cm/s** ($0.2\ \text{m/s}$) and **30 cm/s** ($0.3\ \text{m/s}$).
- **Flow Direction:** Capable of evaluating both **concurrent** (flame spreading in the direction of airflow) and **opposed** (flame spreading against the airflow) burning regimes.
- **Atmospheric Composition:** Cygnus cabin air (~20.9% O$_2$, ~79.1% N$_2$, atmospheric pressure ~101 kPa).
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
### Multi-Sample Card Configuration (9 Samples)
Saffire-II mounted 9 separate material test specimens (each $5\ \text{cm}$ wide by $29\ \text{cm}$ long, matching standard NASA-STD-6001 sample dimensions) on a motorized/indexed sample carrier:
1. **SIBAL Composite Fabric:** 75% cotton / 25% fiberglass blend ($18\ \text{mg/cm}^2$), establishing cross-flight calibration with Saffire-I.
2. **Silicone Sheets (Thin):** Transparent aerospace silicone elastomer representing hatch seals and optical potting.
3. **Silicone Sheets (Thick):** High-temperature silicone gasket elastomer.
4. **Structured PMMA (Polymethyl Methacrylate):** Acrylic slabs machined with longitudinal surface ribs and grooves to evaluate surface geometry effects on flame anchoring.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
5. **Flat Solid PMMA (Thin):** Standard flat cast clear acrylic slab.
6. **Flat Solid PMMA (Thick):** Thermally thick PMMA slab to measure steady-state regression and solid-phase pyrolysis conduction.
7. **PMMA with Nomex Fabric Blend:** Layered sandwich of flammable PMMA with flame-resistant meta-aramid Nomex to evaluate composite fire-retardant barrier mechanics.
8. **Composite Polymer / Fiberglass Blends:** Additional structural composite specimens.
9. **Secondary Verification Specimen:** Opposed-flow calibration strip.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
### In-Flight Instrumentation
- **Dual Camera Systems:** High-resolution digital video cameras capturing color RGB flame propagation, pyrolyzed char boundaries, and soot emissions from top-down and oblique angles.
- **Temperature Rakes:** Arrays of calibrated type-K thermocouples measuring gas-phase flame temperature, solid fuel surface temperature, and duct exhaust gas thermal rise.
- **Radiative Flux Gauges:** Two wide-angle radiometers measuring total radiant heat flux emitted by each burning specimen.
- **Gas Diagnostics:** Electrochemical and non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) sensors measuring oxygen depletion ($\Delta \text{O}_2$) and carbon dioxide accumulation ($\text{CO}_2$).
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text: - **Flow Telemetry:** Dual ultrasonic anemometers monitoring core flow velocity and boundary-layer profiles across the card.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Validation of NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 in Microgravity:**
   - Saffire-II provided the first direct, side-by-side comparison between 1g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 ratings and microgravity flammability for standard-sized ($5\ \text{cm} \times 29\ \text{cm}$) specimens.
   - Proved that low-speed forced flows ($20 - 30\ \text{cm/s}$) in 0g sustain flame propagation over materials near their terrestrial extinction limits because the absence of buoyant convective cooling preserves a high flame temperature near the solid fuel surface.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
2. **Surface Structuring & Ribbed PMMA Phenomena:**
   - Structured PMMA (with machined surface grooves) exhibited significantly faster flame spread rates than flat PMMA slabs.
   - Flow visualization revealed that micro-vortices formed inside the surface grooves, trapping hot pyrolyzed volatiles and augmenting local convective heat flux into the polymer matrix.

3. **Silicone Elastomer Burning & Silica Residue Formation:**
   - Burning silicone specimens formed a porous white silica ($\text{SiO}_2$) ash crust that curled and bubbled.
   - In microgravity, without buoyant buoyancy to detach the crust, the silica ash remained attached to the fuel surface, acting as a dynamic thermal barrier that eventually extinguished the flame via oxygen starvation and insulation.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
4. **Thermally Thick PMMA Regression & 3D Pyrolysis Models:**
   - Thick PMMA demonstrated steady concurrent spread driven by solid-phase thermal conduction and gas-phase radiation feedback.
   - Data validated 3D solid pyrolysis and gas-phase Navier-Stokes models developed by UC Berkeley (Thomsen and Fernandez-Pello) and CWRU (Li, Liao, and T'ien), showing exact agreement in mass loss rate and flame base velocity.

---

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
---

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Spacecraft Material Screening Protocol Overhaul:**
   - Confirmed that terrestrial 1g flammability testing is non-conservative for certain geometric configurations (ribbed, textured, or multi-layer materials) under low-velocity spacecraft cabin ventilation.
   - Led to recommendations that materials certified for long-duration exploration vehicles (Orion, Gateway, Lunar surface habitats) must account for low-gravity forced-convection boundary layer effects.
title: NASA PSI-99: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II Multi-Material Low-Gravity Flammability)

text:
2. **Ventilation System Flow-Velocity Thresholds:**
   - Saffire-II confirmed that reducing cabin airflow velocity from $30\ \text{cm/s}$ to $20\ \text{cm/s}$ reduced flame spread velocity ($V_f$) and flame length, demonstrating that emergency cabin ventilation shutdowns ("choke flow" procedures) remain a primary fire mitigation tactic.

3. **Multi-Sensor Fire Detection Signatures:**
   - Co-registered sensor data from Saffire-II provided empirical source-term signatures ($\text{CO}$, $\text{CO}_2$, optical soot scattering, and thermal rise) across multiple distinct engineering polymers, enabling the tuning of multi-criteria detector alarm algorithms for human spacecraft.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Smoke Point Physics Rationale
The **laminar smoke point** is a fundamental combustion parameter defining the maximum fuel flow rate or flame length at which a non-premixed flame completely oxidizes all soot internally without releasing smoke particles through the flame tip. When fuel flow exceeds the smoke point, unoxidized soot particulates escape into the surroundings, generating hazardous smoke aerosols and unburned toxic hydrocarbons.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text: On Earth, natural buoyancy ($Gr \gg 1$) accelerates hot gases upward through the flame at speeds of $1.0 - 2.0\ \text{m/s}$, inducing high velocity strain rates that shorten fluid residence times and enhance air entrainment. Buoyant smoke points are governed primarily by Froude-number scaling ($Fr = u^2 / g L$).
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text:
In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, buoyancy is eliminated ($Gr \to 0$). Gas transport is dictated strictly by low-speed forced coflow air and fuel jet momentum:
1. **Prolonged Residence Times:** Gas residence times in microgravity diffusion flames are an order of magnitude longer than in buoyant flames, allowing soot precursor particles (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, PAHs) to spend extensive time in the high-temperature fuel-rich pyrolysis zone.
2. **Soot Production vs Oxidation Balance:** Soot formation scales with local temperature and residence time, while soot oxidation requires molecular oxygen transport through the flame sheet. Without buoyant mixing, the smoke point occurs at fundamentally different fuel flow rates and flame lengths.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text: 3. **Spacecraft Radiative Hazard:** Sooting flames in microgravity lose a massive proportion of their heat release through continuum thermal radiation ($\sim 35 - 45\%$, compared to $\sim 10 - 15\%$ on Earth), presenting severe radiative ignition risks to surrounding spacecraft components.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)
NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text:
## 3. Flight Architecture & The SPICE Apparatus
The SPICE investigation operated inside the **Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)** in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:
- **Burner Assembly:** Precision exchangeable stainless-steel circular fuel nozzles with internal diameters of:
  - $d_1 = 0.41\ \text{mm}$ (small burner)
  - $d_2 = 0.76\ \text{mm}$ (medium burner)
  - $d_3 = 1.60\ \text{mm}$ (large burner)
- **Coflow Flow Duct:** Vertical flow duct delivering conditioned, laminar coflow air at velocities ranging from **$5.4\ \text{cm/s}$ to $65.0\ \text{cm/s}$**, simulating the entire operational velocity range of spacecraft cabin ventilation systems.
- **Hydrocarbon Fuels Investigated:**
  - Methane ($\text{CH}_4$): Baseline non-sooting hydrocarbon.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text:
- Methane ($\text{CH}_4$): Baseline non-sooting hydrocarbon.
  - Ethylene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$): Standard high-sooting alkene.
  - Propane ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$): Standard alkane fuel.
  - Propylene ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$) and propylene / fuel mixtures: Probing chemical structure effects on soot nucleation.
- **Flight Test Matrix Scope:**
  - A staggering total of **526 distinct laminar diffusion flames** were ignited and analyzed in microgravity, establishing one of the largest empirical datasets in NASA combustion history.
- **Diagnostics & Instrumentation:**
  - High-resolution color CCD cameras capturing calibrated still images and video sequences of flame height, luminous soot zone, and smoke emissions.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text:
- Broadband and narrowband radiometers measuring radiant heat loss fractions.
  - Hot-wire anemometry measuring coflow velocity profiles and turbulence intensity across the duct cross section.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Laminar Smoke Point Scaling Laws in 0g:**
   - SPICE established that non-buoyant smoke-point flame lengths and critical fuel mass flow rates scale inversely with coflow velocity:
     $$L_{\text{sp}} \propto \frac{1}{u_{\text{coflow}}}$$
     confirming residence-time scaling rather than the Froude-number scaling that governs terrestrial buoyant flames.
   - For a given fuel and burner diameter, as coflow velocity is decreased, the smoke point occurs at progressively smaller fuel flow rates. At very low coflow speeds ($< 10\ \text{cm/s}$), flames emit soot at exceptionally small fuel flow rates.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text:
2. **Microgravity Soot Inception & Flame Geometry:**
   - In 0g, diffusion flames widen by a factor of 2x to 3x, and the soot inception zone moves closer to the burner exit rim compared to 1g.
   - Soot volume fractions in microgravity ethylene and propylene flames were measured to be 2x to 4x higher than in equivalent normal-gravity flames due to reduced scalar dissipation and extended residence times.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text:
3. **Radiative Fraction & Quenching:**
   - Radiant heat loss from luminous soot reached up to **35% to 45%** of the total heat of combustion in microgravity.
   - At high fuel flow rates or low coflow velocities, excessive radiative heat loss caused the flame tip to cool below $1200\ \text{K}$, leading to radiative tip-quenching and massive emission of unburned soot and carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$).

4. **Validation of Yale & Michigan Soot Models:**
   - Flight data validated the 2D coflow diffusion flame models developed by Smooke, Long, and Faeth, confirming that sectional soot aerosol models accurately reproduce soot volume fraction and smoke point thresholds when informed by non-buoyant transport equations.

1. **Spacecraft Cabin Gas Leak Flammability & Smoke Hazards:**
   - Confirmed that gaseous fuel leaks in spacecraft cabins will transition to smoking, soot-emitting flames at significantly lower mass leak rates than on Earth.
   - The large soot particles emitted by microgravity flames readily foul ECLSS ventilation filters and emergency catalytic oxidizers.

2. **Radiative Heat Transfer to Spacecraft Materials:**
   - Because microgravity flames lose over one-third of their energy as thermal radiation from the soot zone, nearby structural materials and cabling will receive severe radiative heating even without direct flame impingement, accelerating fire growth and secondary ignitions.
title: NASA PSI-107: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE ISS Diffusion Flame Investigation)

text:
3. **Sensor Calibration for Incipient Gas Fires:**
   - Confirmed that optical soot scattering detectors will see strong early smoke signals from gaseous jet fires in microgravity, but gas-phase $\text{CO}$ and $\text{CO}_2$ sensors are essential to detect clean-burning methane leaks before smoke-point breakthrough occurs.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Fire Scaling Rationale
The **Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (Saffire-III)** was the critical third flight in NASA's Saffire series, conducted aboard the uncrewed Cygnus CRS OA-7 cargo vehicle after completing its ISS resupply mission and unberthing into autonomous free flight.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text: While Saffire-I (PSI-98) demonstrated the feasibility of igniting and monitoring a large-scale solid fabric fire ($0.94\ \text{m} \times 0.40\ \text{m}$) in microgravity under a nominal cabin ventilation flow of **20 cm/s** ($0.2\ \text{m/s}$), **Saffire-III** was designed to investigate the direct effect of **elevated airflow velocity** on large-scale fire growth and spread kinetics:
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
1. **Flow Velocity Scaling:** Forced airflow in spacecraft cabins typically ranges from $0.05\ \text{m/s}$ to $0.40\ \text{m/s}$. Increasing forced flow velocity delivers fresh oxygen to the flame base at a higher mass flux, which enhances chemical heat release. However, it simultaneously increases convective cooling and gas-phase residence time shear. Resolving whether higher airflow accelerates flame spread or induces flame thinning and quench is paramount for spacecraft emergency ventilation management.
2. **Elevated Velocity Burn (30 cm/s):** Saffire-III ignited an identical large-scale solid composite fabric under an elevated concurrent airflow velocity of **30 cm/s** ($0.3\ \text{m/s}$), providing the empirical counterpart to Saffire-I.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text: 3. **Validation of Transient Numerical Models:** The data provided direct validation for transient 2D and 3D Navier-Stokes combustion models developed by CWRU, UC Berkeley, and NASA GRC to predict how forced ventilation drives large fire progression in future exploration spacecraft (Orion, Lunar Gateway, Mars transit).
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 3. Flight Architecture & The SAFFIRE-III Experiment

### Flight Hardware & Flow Duct
- **Platform:** Orbital ATK Cygnus CRS OA-7 (*SS John Glenn*) cargo vehicle operating in low Earth orbit before destructive atmospheric re-entry.
- **Combustion Duct:** A dedicated flow tunnel measuring $0.9\ \text{m} \times 0.5\ \text{m} \times 1.4\ \text{m}$ installed in the Cygnus pressurized module.
- **Flow Conditioning:** Suction fans and flow straighteners established a controlled, uniform concurrent airflow velocity of **30 cm/s** across the fuel surface.
- **Ambient Atmosphere:** Cygnus cabin atmosphere (~20.9% O$_2$, ~79.1% N$_2$, nominal pressure ~101 kPa).
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
### Test Material Specification
- **Fuel Sample:** A large composite fabric known as **SIBAL**:
  - Composition: 75% cotton / 25% fiberglass blend by weight.
  - Dimensions: **0.94 meters long by 0.40 meters wide** ($94\ \text{cm} \times 40\ \text{cm}$).
  - Areal Density: Nominally $18\ \text{mg/cm}^2$.
  - Behavior: The cotton pyrolyzes and burns cleanly, while the inert fiberglass woven matrix retains structural integrity after combustion, preventing flying embers or aerodynamic fuel curling in the 30 cm/s flow.
- **Ignition Source:** Uniform line ignition triggered by an electrically energized continuous Kanthal hot-wire along the upstream leading edge.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
### In-Flight Instrumentation & Diagnostics
- **Calibrated Multi-Camera Imaging:** High-resolution digital video cameras capturing synchronized color imaging of the flame front, pyrolyzing char line, luminous soot emissions, and flame standoff distance.
- **Thermal Diagnostic Rakes:** Arrays of fast-response type-K thermocouples measuring leading-edge flow temperature, flame zone gas temperature, and duct exhaust gas thermal rise.
- **Radiative Flux Gauges:** Wide-angle and narrow-angle radiometers measuring continuous radiant heat flux emitted from the flame sheet toward the fuel surface and enclosure walls.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
- **Gas Diagnostics:** High-precision solid-state, electrochemical, and NDIR sensors recording oxygen depletion ($\Delta \text{O}_2$), carbon dioxide accumulation ($\text{CO}_2$), and carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$).
- **Flow Metrology:** Ultrasonic anemometers continuously logging duct velocity profiles and boundary-layer stability.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Velocity Dependency of Flame Spread Rate ($V_f$):**
   - At 30 cm/s concurrent flow, the flame spread rate over the SIBAL fabric increased to **$V_f \approx 0.38 - 0.45\ \text{cm/s}$**, compared to $0.28 - 0.32\ \text{cm/s}$ observed at 20 cm/s in Saffire-I.
   - The increased convective mass flux of oxygen enhanced the chemical heat release rate at the flame base, overpowering the modest increase in convective cooling.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Flame Geometry & Luminous Sheet Elongation:**
   - The 30 cm/s airflow stretched the flame sheet downstream, producing a continuous, luminous trailing flame exceeding **35 cm in length**.
   - The longer flame sheet dramatically increased the view factor and total radiative preheating flux delivered to the virgin solid fuel ahead of the pyrolysis front, sustaining rapid, uninterrupted forward spread.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
3. **Complete Fuel Consumption & Structural Char Stability:**
   - The flame consumed all cotton fibers along the entire 0.94-meter length in approximately 4.5 minutes.
   - The fiberglass matrix remained fully intact without tearing, confirming that properly engineered structural fire barriers can withstand elevated low-gravity airflow without fragmenting into hazardous airborne debris.

4. **Transient Navier-Stokes Model Validation:**
   - Flight telemetry validated 2D and 3D numerical models developed by Li, Liao, and T'ien (CWRU). Model predictions of flame base position versus time, pyrolyzed mass consumption rate, and cabin oxygen depletion kinetics matched experimental observations within $< 6\%$ error across both 20 cm/s and 30 cm/s test runs.

---
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Spacecraft Ventilation Control Protocols:**
   - Comparing Saffire-I (20 cm/s) and Saffire-III (30 cm/s) provided conclusive empirical evidence that higher ventilation velocities accelerate flame spread and fire intensity in microgravity.
   - Reaffirmed that **immediate cabin ventilation shutdown** is the most effective operational intervention to depressurize the convective oxygen flux, decelerate flame propagation, and facilitate fire suppression.
title: NASA PSI-100: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III Elevated Flow Velocity Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Refining Exploration Flammability Criteria:**
   - Proved that low-gravity flammability is highly sensitive to ventilation boundary layers. Materials screened on Earth under 1g natural convection must be re-evaluated under forced-flow conditions relevant to exploration atmospheres (e.g., 34% O$_2$ at 8.2 psia for Artemis Lunar missions).

3. **ECLSS Emergency Scrubbing & Sensor Placement:**
   - Saffire-III documented rapid cabin oxygen depletion and massive CO/CO$_2$ release rates under elevated airflow. These findings define the minimum volumetric scrubbing capacity required for Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) and Emergency Mask Systems (EMS) during contingency recovery.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Diffusion Flame Physics Rationale
Non-premixed laminar diffusion flames are ubiquitous in energy conversion systems and represent the primary physical model for gas jet leaks and fires in aerospace vehicles. On Earth, natural buoyancy-driven convection ($Gr \gg 1$) accelerates hot gases upward at $1.0 - 2.0\ \text{m/s}$, inducing strong velocity shear at the burner rim that narrows the reaction zone and compresses fluid residence times. This buoyancy-dominated flow obscures the fundamental interactions between molecular diffusion, chemical reaction kinetics, and soot aerosol dynamics.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, buoyancy is eliminated ($Gr \to 0$). Fluid flow is governed entirely by fuel jet momentum and low-speed forced coflow air. The **ACME Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame** investigation was designed to conduct rigorous experimental evaluations of diffusion flames across the extremes of the fuel dilution and sooting spectrum:
1. **Weak Dilute Flames:** Characterizing the extinction limits, liftoff heights, and flame base stabilization mechanisms of highly diluted methane and ethylene flames as a function of coflow velocity and nitrogen dilution.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
2. **Heavily Sooting Flames:** Examining soot inception, surface growth, agglomeration, and radiative emissions in flames with long residence times, measuring soot temperatures and soot volume fractions ($f_v$).
3. **Computational Validation:** Providing benchmark microgravity experimental datasets to test and refine high-order 2D and 3D computational fluid dynamics models coupling detailed chemical kinetics with sectional soot aerosol dynamics.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)
NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

## 3. Flight Architecture & The ACME Hardware
The ACME CLD Flame investigation was conducted within the **Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)** using the modular **Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)** insert in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:
- **Combustion Chamber:** Hermetically sealed chamber supporting controlled gas atmospheres from sub-atmospheric pressures up to elevated pressures.
- **Burner Assembly:** Coaxial burner featuring a centered circular fuel tube surrounded by an axisymmetric honeycomb coflow air delivery nozzle supplying uniform, low-velocity laminar oxidizer streams.
- **Fuels & Dilutions Tested:**
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
- **Fuels & Dilutions Tested:**
  - Methane ($\text{CH}_4$) and ethylene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$) across an extensive spectrum of nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$) dilution—from pure hydrocarbon fuel down to near-extinction dilute mixtures ($< 15\%\ \text{fuel} / > 85\%\ \text{N}_2$).
- **Advanced Optical Diagnostics:**
  - **Chemiluminescence Imaging:** High-sensitivity cameras capturing spontaneous emission from excited hydroxyl ($\text{OH}^*$) and methylidyne ($\text{CH}^*$) radicals to resolve the flame anchor zone, liftoff height, and flame sheet geometry.
  - **Laser-Induced Incandescence (LII) & Laser Extinction:** Determining 2D spatial distributions of soot volume fraction ($f_v$) and soot particle morphology.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
- **Color-Ratio Pyrometry & Thin-Filament Pyrometry (TFP):** Employing silicon carbide (SiC) filaments to measure 2D gas temperature fields in non-sooting flame regions and soot emission temperatures in sooting lobes.
  - **Broadband Radiometers:** Measuring total radiant heat loss fraction ($F_{\text{rad}}$) emitted from the flame to the chamber walls.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Flame Widening & Stabilization Envelope in 0g:**
   - In microgravity, diffusion flames expand radially by a factor of 2x to 3x compared to normal gravity flames due to the absence of buoyant constriction.
   - The elimination of buoyant shear strain at the burner base allows flames to remain anchored at substantially higher fuel exit velocities, dramatically broadening the stable burner operating envelope.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
2. **Fuel Dilution Transitions & Soot Inception:**
   - Systematic nitrogen dilution lowered peak flame temperatures and delayed the onset of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) soot precursors.
   - Microgravity ethylene flames transitioned smoothly from intensely luminous yellow sooting flames to translucent blue, soot-free flames as dilution increased, establishing precise chemical threshold boundaries for soot inception without buoyant interference.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
3. **Radiative Tip Quenching & Soot Breakthrough:**
   - Because residence times in microgravity are prolonged by an order of magnitude, soot particles experience extensive surface growth and agglomeration, causing radiative heat loss from soot to reach **30% to 45%** of total combustion energy.
   - At high fuel flow rates or low coflow velocities, extreme radiative cooling cooled the flame tip below $1200\ \text{K}$, leading to "tip-opening" and the continuous emission of unoxidized carbon soot into the ambient environment.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
4. **Benchmark Model Validation (18 Archival Papers):**
   - Experimental flame shapes, $\text{CH}^*$ radical distributions, temperature profiles, and soot volume fractions provided benchmark validation for 2D parallelized Navier-Stokes combustion codes developed by Smooke, Long, and Bennett. Numerical models achieved extraordinary agreement with experimental flame heights and liftoff velocities ($< 5\%$ error).

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Spacecraft Cabin Gas Leak Flammability:**
   - Pressurized gas lines (hydrogen, methane, ethylene) are utilized across spacecraft propulsion, fuel cell systems, and scientific payloads. ACME CLD Flame proved that microgravity gas leaks ignite and sustain stable diffusion flames at lower flow speeds and broader dilution ranges than on Earth.

2. **Radiative Flashover Hazard:**
   - The large surface area and high radiative fraction (up to 45%) of microgravity diffusion flames generate intense radiant heat flux that can warm neighboring avionics and structural polymers to their pyrolysis threshold, accelerating fire spread across spacecraft compartments.
title: NASA PSI-21: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)

text:
3. **Soot Filter Loading & Life Support Protection:**
   - Tip-quenching and soot emission from low-gravity gas fires produce large soot agglomerates that rapidly blind ECLSS smoke removal filters and contaminate air revitalization catalysts.

## 2. Executive Summary & Microgravity Solid Fuel Combustion Physics
The **Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II)** experiment was the definitive microgravity solid fuel combustion investigation conducted aboard the International Space Station to bridge the gap between terrestrial flammability screening (**NASA-STD-6001 Test 1**) and actual material burning behavior in spaceflight environments.
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
On Earth, buoyancy-driven natural convection creates an upward draft of $1.0 - 2.0\ \text{m/s}$ that accelerates upward fire growth over vertical fuels. Consequently, NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screens materials using upward burning in normal gravity, considering it the "worst-case" flammability scenario. However:
1. **The Flammability Paradox in Microgravity:** In the absence of buoyancy, gas transport is dictated by low-velocity forced ventilation ($0.01 - 0.40\ \text{m/s}$). While buoyant cooling and air entrainment quench terrestrial flames near extinction limits, the low convective heat loss in microgravity allows solid fuels to burn vigorously at low airflow speeds.
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Hypothesis Tested:** BASS-II tested the hypothesis that with adequate low-speed ventilation, solid materials in microgravity burn as well as, or faster than, identical materials in normal gravity under identical atmospheric conditions (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature).
3. **Multi-Geometry & Solid Fuel Spectrum:** Evaluated practical, thicker fuels across varied geometric forms: flat slabs, solid cylindrical rods, spherical sections, thin films, and composite fabrics under both **opposed flow** (flame advancing against the flow) and **concurrent flow** (flame advancing with the flow).
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)
NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
## 3. Flight Architecture & The BASS-II Apparatus
Operated inside the **Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)** in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS with active astronaut crew collaboration:
- **Small Wind Tunnel:** Enclosed flow duct installed inside the MSG capable of imposing precisely controlled forced airflows from **$0.5\ \text{cm/s}$ up to $40.0\ \text{cm/s}$**.
- **Working Atmosphere Control:** Nitrogen vitiation to reduce ambient oxygen mole fraction from 21% down to limiting oxygen concentrations ($\approx 13 - 15\%\ \text{O}_2$) to determine absolute flammability boundaries.
- **Tested Solid Fuels & Geometries:**
  - **PMMA (Polymethyl Methacrylate):** Cylindrical solid rods ($d = 6.35\ \text{mm}$, $9.5\ \text{mm}$), flat slabs, and thin cast sheets.
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
- **Cellulose / Thin Fuel Sheets:** Whatman filter paper and thin cellulosic films.
  - **SIBAL Composite Fabric:** Cotton-fiberglass woven blend sheets.
  - **Delrin / POM (Polyoxymethylene):** Standard aerospace engineering thermoplastic rods and slabs.
- **Diagnostics & Telemetry:**
  - High-resolution digital video cameras capturing synchronized color and near-IR flame morphology, standoff distance, and regression rates.
  - On-board Compound Specific Analyzer - Combustion Products (CSA-CP) and Carbon Dioxide Monitor (CDM) measuring in-cabin combustion effluent gases.
  - Thermocouple rakes measuring gas and solid surface temperatures.
  - Over 694 high-resolution video and telemetry files archived (**274.6 GB total**).
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
1. **Identification of Opposed-Flow Flame Spread Regimes:**
   - BASS-II clearly mapped three distinct regimes for opposed-flow flame spread over PMMA and cellulose in microgravity:
     - *Radiative Extinction Regime (Low Flow, $u < 5\ \text{cm/s}$):* At extremely low flow speeds, radiative heat loss from the flame sheet overpowers chemical heat release, causing the flame to extinguish.
     - *Thermal Regime (Intermediate Flow, $5 < u < 25\ \text{cm/s}$):* Flame spread velocity is nearly constant or weakly dependent on velocity, governed by a balance of forward gas conduction and solid-phase thermal heat capacity.
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text: - *Kinetic / Blowoff Regime (High Flow, $u > 30\ \text{cm/s}$):* High velocity strain thins the reaction zone at the flame base, shortening residence time and culminating in convective blowoff.
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **PMMA Rod Flammability & Stagnation Flow Boundaries:**
   - PMMA rods burning in axial stagnation flow demonstrated that the limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) in microgravity is significantly lower at low forced flow velocities than in normal gravity.
   - Flames formed rounded hemispherical caps over the rod tips, burning stably at flow velocities where terrestrial buoyant flames extinguish.

3. **Inadequacy of NASA-STD-6001 Test 1:**
   - Proved empirically that materials rated self-extinguishing or non-flammable under terrestrial 1g upward testing can sustain steady, propagating flames in microgravity under low-speed forced ventilation ($10 - 20\ \text{cm/s}$).
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
4. **Extensive Validation of Numerical Models (17 Archival Papers):**
   - Experimental flame base profiles, temperature fields, and spread rates provided benchmark validation for 2D/3D numerical models developed by SDSU (Bhattacharjee), CWRU (T'ien, Liao), and UC Berkeley (Fernandez-Pello).

---

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Spacecraft Cabin Material Selection:**
   - Provided the definitive scientific foundation for the NASA Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) program and future exploration vehicle material certifications.
   - Proved that spacecraft material flammability cannot be predicted from 1g tests alone; forced-flow boundary layer interactions must be accounted for in spacecraft habitats.
title: NASA PSI-25: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II Solid Fuel Flight Investigation)

text:
2. **Ventilation Shutdown & Suppression Tactics:**
   - Established that reducing cabin forced ventilation below the critical radiative extinction limit ($u < 2 - 5\ \text{cm/s}$) triggers radiative quench of opposed-flow flames, validating ventilation shutdown as an effective fire suppression protocol in air with 21% O$_2$.

3. **Post-Fire Scrubbing & Toxic Product Yields:**
   - On-board CSA-CP and CDM data quantified real-time carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and soot emission rates from pyrolyzing aerospace polymers, setting engineering design rules for ECLSS post-fire cabin atmosphere revitalization.

## 2. Executive Summary & Condensed-Phase Emulation Physics
Evaluating the flammability of solid and liquid fuels in microgravity is complicated by solid-phase phenomena such as melting, dripping, bubbling, char formation, and surface regression. The **Burning Rate Emulator (BRE)** is an innovative combustion apparatus designed to simulate the burning of condensed-phase fuels (such as PMMA, polyoxymethylene, and nylon) without condensed-phase mass regression.
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
The BRE emulates condensed-phase fuels by injecting gaseous fuel mixtures (methane/nitrogen $\text{CH}_4/\text{N}_2$ or ethylene/nitrogen $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4/\text{N}_2$) through a porous sintered copper circular burner. By matching the gaseous mixture's properties to the condensed fuel's thermochemical parameters:
$$\text{Heat of Gasification } (L_v),\quad \text{Heat of Combustion } (\Delta H_c),\quad \text{and Smoke Point}$$
the burner accurately emulates real solid fuel combustion while embedded surface thermocouples and heat flux gauges directly measure the net energy returned from the flame to the fuel surface:
$$\dot{q}''_{net} = \dot{q}''_{conv} + \dot{q}''_{rad} - \epsilon \sigma T_s^4$$
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
### The Quiescent Exploration Atmosphere Challenge
A long-standing assumption in spacecraft fire safety is that stopping cabin airflow (ventilation shutdown) will extinguish solid fires in microgravity due to oxygen starvation and stagnant diffusive choking. BRE investigated whether this assumption holds in future NASA Exploration Atmospheres designed for Artemis, Gateway, and lunar habitats:
1. **Standard Sea-Level Air:** 14.7 psia ($101.3\ \text{kPa}$), 21% O$_2$, balance N$_2$.
2. **Intermediate Air (Pre-EVA):** 10.2 psia ($70.3\ \text{kPa}$), 26.5% O$_2$, balance N$_2$.
3. **Exploration Atmosphere (Artemis / Lunar):** 8.2 psia ($56.5\ \text{kPa}$), 34% O$_2$, balance N$_2$.

---
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
## 3. Flight Architecture & The BRE Experimental Apparatus
Deployed in the **Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)** using the **ACME** chamber insert in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:
- **Porous Burners:** Sintered copper porous circular burners with diameters of **$25\ \text{mm}$** and **$50\ \text{mm}$** mounted flush within an insulated ceramic holder.
- **Surface Diagnostics:** Embedded Schmidt-Boelter heat flux gauges and sub-surface calibrated thermocouples recording continuous heat feedback ($\dot{q}''_{net}$) and burner surface temperature ($T_s$).
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
- **Gaseous Emulation Fuel Delivery:** Mass flow controllers delivering precise flows of $\text{CH}_4/\text{N}_2$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4/\text{N}_2$ to emulate the effective vaporization rate ($\dot{m}'' = \dot{q}''_{net} / L_v$) of real materials including PMMA, POM, and Nylon.
- **Chamber Environment:** Quiescent (zero forced velocity) and low-velocity forced flows across varying pressure and oxygen concentrations ($15\%\ \text{to}\ 34\%\ \text{O}_2$).
- **Optical Diagnostics:** High-resolution digital color video, narrow-band chemiluminescence tracking flame standoff and diameter, and radiometers measuring radiant heat loss.
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Quasi-Steady Burning in Quiescent Air (The Exploration Atmosphere Hazard):**
   - In standard 21% O$_2$ air at 14.7 psia, flames burning over the BRE in quiescent microgravity rapidly decayed and self-extinguished within 30 to 60 seconds due to oxygen starvation and radiative cooling.
   - In **elevated-oxygen exploration atmospheres (34% O$_2$ at 8.2 psia)**, flames corresponding to solid materials like **PMMA and Nylon achieved stable, quasi-steady spherical burning without any airflow**.
   - This empirically disproved the universal validity of ventilation shutdown: in exploration atmospheres with enriched oxygen, solid materials can continue burning indefinitely via pure molecular diffusion.
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
2. **Flammability Maps & Steady-State Heat Flux:**
   - BRE generated complete multi-dimensional flammability maps correlating emulated material properties ($L_v$, $\Delta H_c$, smoke point) with measured surface heat flux ($\dot{q}''_{net}$).
   - Demonstrated that steady burning is achieved when the energy returned from the flame equals the energy required to vaporize the fuel plus reradiative surface losses.

3. **Validation of NASA Flammability Test 2 (Cone Calorimeter):**
   - Results proved that data from the terrestrial Cone Calorimeter (**NASA-STD-6001 Test 2**) can be directly mapped to low-gravity burning through the BRE framework, providing a viable alternative to the non-conservative upward burning Test 1.
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
4. **Transient Radiative Extinction Modeling:**
   - Data validated transient ellipsoidal and spherical numerical combustion models (Markan, Baum, Sunderland, de Ris, and Snegirev), confirming theoretical predictions of radiative extinction boundaries in stagnant microgravity.

---

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Artemis & Lunar Habitat Fire Safety Architecture:**
   - The finding that materials burn stably in 34% O$_2$ / 8.2 psia exploration atmospheres without forced flow fundamentally alters spacecraft emergency procedures. Fire suppression in lunar habitats cannot rely solely on switching off the fans; active fire suppression agents (such as fine water mist or $\text{CO}_2$) are mandatory to extinguish quiescent flames.
title: NASA PSI-20: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)

text:
2. **Cone Calorimeter Screening Standard:**
   - Strongly supports transitioning NASA and commercial material flight certification from qualitative pass/fail upward flame tests to quantitative property measurements using the Cone Calorimeter.

3. **Sensor Response to Stagnant Spherical Flames:**
   - In quiescent microgravity, flames form broad, rounded ellipsoids that produce steady, hemispherical smoke and gas clouds. Fire detectors must be placed to intercept diffusion transport when ventilation is deactivated.

---

## 2. Executive Summary & Droplet Extinguishment Physics
Droplet combustion serves as the classical canonical model for liquid spray combustion in gas turbines, rocket engines, diesel powerplants, and accidental liquid fuel leaks aboard spacecraft. On Earth, natural buoyancy-driven convection ($Gr \gg 1$) distorts droplet flames into upwardly directed plumes, sweeps away soot, and induces forced convective evaporation that masks liquid-phase mass transport.
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, isolated fuel droplets burn with near-perfect spherical symmetry. The **Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2)** significantly expanded the discoveries of FLEX-1 by investigating droplet burning under conditions that mimic realistic industrial fuels and complex combustion environments:
1. **Bi-Component Droplet Combustion & Liquid-Phase Diffusion:** Real liquid fuels are complex multi-component mixtures. FLEX-2 studied bi-component droplets (e.g., heptane/hexadecane, butanol/gasoline surrogates) to observe internal liquid-phase mass diffusion, preferential vaporization, and micro-explosion/puffing phenomena.
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
2. **Droplet Arrays & Interaction Effects:** In practical sprays, droplets do not burn in isolation. FLEX-2 evaluated binary linear droplet arrays, varying droplet spacing to study flammability limits and collective extinction boundaries.
3. **Convective Droplet Combustion:** Evaluated translating droplets subjected to controlled relative motion ($0.01 - 0.2\ \text{m/s}$) to measure the transition from spherically symmetric burning to wake flames.
4. **Cool Flame Transitions & Extinction Limits:** Investigated the transition between hot-flame burning ($T > 1500\ \text{K}$), radiative extinction, and self-sustaining low-temperature cool flame combustion ($T \approx 600 - 1000\ \text{K}$).
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)
NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

## 3. Flight Architecture & The FLEX-2 Hardware
Operated within the **Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)** using the **Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)** in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:
- **Combustion Chamber Atmosphere:** 100-liter chamber with pressures varied from **$0.5\ \text{atm}$ to $3.0\ \text{atm}$**; ambient oxygen mole fractions from **10% to 40% O$_2$** diluted with nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$), helium ($\text{He}$), or carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$).
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
- **Droplet Dispensing & Deployment:** High-precision automated syringe needles dispensing single droplets ($d_0 \approx 1.5 - 5.0\ \text{mm}$) deployed freely floating in space or tethered between ultra-fine silicon carbide (SiC, $14\ \mu\text{m}$) fibers. Linear arrays deployed two interacting droplets with variable center-to-center spacing.
- **Tested Hydrocarbon & Alcohol Fuels:**
  - Pure alkanes: $n$-heptane, $n$-octane, $n$-decane, $n$-dodecane, and $n$-hexadecane.
  - Biofuels & alcohols: $n$-butanol, ethanol, and alcohol/alkane blends.
  - Complex binary surrogates: $n$-heptane / $n$-hexadecane and butanol/gasoline mixtures.

- **Diagnostics & Imaging Systems:**

  - Low-Light / Intensified UV Cameras recording $\text{OH}^*$ and $\text{CH}^*$ chemiluminescence and flame dimensions.
  - High-speed color video capturing soot shell dynamics and droplet internal motion.
  - Narrow-band and broadband radiometers measuring radiant heat loss fractions.
  - Over **1.225 Terabytes** of flight data archived.
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
---

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Quasi-Steady Cool Flame Verification Across Alkane Families:**
   - FLEX-2 proved that the second-stage cool flame phenomenon is universal across intermediate and heavy $n$-alkanes ($n$-octane through $n$-hexadecane).
   - Following radiative extinction of the hot flame, droplets continue to burn in a cool flame mode supported by low-temperature alkylperoxy chemistry, with burning rate constants $K_{\text{cool}} \approx (0.25 - 0.5) K_{\text{hot}}$.
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
2. **Liquid-Phase Mass Diffusion Resistance in Bi-Component Droplets:**
   - In mixtures of fuels with disparate boiling points (e.g., $n$-heptane and $n$-hexadecane), liquid-phase mass diffusion inside the droplet is slower than surface regression ($Pe_L \gg 1$).
   - This diffusion resistance produces surface depletion of the more volatile component, driving sudden shifts in flame temperature, burning rate, and soot shell structure during droplet lifetime.
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
3. **Soot Shell Formation & Radiative Extinction:**
   - In microgravity, thermophoresis drives soot particles outward from the hot flame zone, where they accumulate in a dense, spherical "soot shell" between the droplet surface and the flame sheet.
   - Radiative heat loss from the soot shell overpowers chemical heat release at critical extinction diameters ($d_{\text{ext}}$), forcing the hot flame to extinguish.

4. **Droplet Interaction Effects in Linear Arrays:**
   - Droplet arrays demonstrated that proximity between droplets reduces oxygen transport to the inner zone while trapping fuel vapor, shifting the array flammability boundary and leading to merged envelope flames at small separation distances.

title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Liquid Fuel Leak & Spray Fire Hazards in Spacecraft:**
   - Spacecraft carry complex multi-component liquid propellants, hydraulic fluids, and thermal coolants. FLEX-2 established that liquid droplet leaks burn stably in microgravity at oxygen levels far lower than predicted by terrestrial 1g tests.
   - Cool flame burning allows liquid fuel droplets to continue vaporizing and reacting without emitting visible light or strong thermal infrared radiation.
title: NASA PSI-68: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2 ISS Droplet Combustion Investigation)

text:
2. **Flashover Re-Ignition Risks:**
   - Confirmed that surviving cool flame reaction zones can reignite into explosive hot flames if cabin airflow or oxygen concentration fluctuates, dictating that spacecraft fire suppression systems must target low-temperature reaction kinetics.

3. **Fire Suppression Agent Modeling:**
   - Data on droplet extinction under varying $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{N}_2$ dilution provides empirical benchmarks for designing spacecraft water mist suppression systems and gaseous total-flooding systems.

## 2. Executive Summary & Electrostatic Flame Physics Rationale
Hydrocarbon combustion naturally produces charged species (positive ions such as $\text{CHO}^+$ and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, alongside free electrons $\text{e}^-$) through high-temperature **chemi-ionization reactions**:
$$\text{CH} + \text{O} \to \text{CHO}^+ + \text{e}^-$$
$$\text{CHO}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{CO} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$$
When an external electric field ($\mathbf{E}$) is applied across a flame, these ions experience an electrostatic body force ($\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{E}$). As the ions accelerate and collide with surrounding neutral gas molecules, they transfer momentum, inducing a bulk gas motion termed the **ion-driven wind** or **ionic wind**.
title: NASA PSI-22: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames)

text:
On Earth, buoyancy-driven natural convection ($1.0 - 2.0\ \text{m/s}$) completely overwhelms this subtle ion-driven momentum transfer. In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, buoyancy is eliminated ($Gr \to 0$). The **ACME E-FIELD Flames** investigation took advantage of this unique environment to cleanly isolate and study the fundamental interactions between electric fields, chemi-ion transport, flame stabilization, and soot emissions:
1. **Ion-Driven Convective Flow:** Quantifying how DC electric fields generate targeted convective flows that reshape, stretch, or compress diffusion flames in the absence of gravity.
title: NASA PSI-22: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames)

text:
2. **Current-Voltage ($I-V$) Response:** Measuring chemi-ion current through the flame as a function of field strength, fuel composition, and electrode polarity up to high voltages (10 kV).
3. **Electrostatic Soot Manipulation:** Determining how electric fields can alter the trajectories of nascent charged soot particles to either suppress soot breakthrough or enhance soot oxidation.
4. **Active Flame Suppression & Stability:** Exploring non-intrusive electrical actuation as an active method to manipulate flame liftoff and force flame extinction without chemical suppressants.
title: NASA PSI-22: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames)
NASA PSI-22: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames)

Operated within the **Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)** using the **ACME** chamber insert in the US Destiny Laboratory on the ISS:

  - *Gas-Jet Burner:* Small circular nozzle producing focused non-premixed flames for high-resolution ion-driven convection studies.
  - *Coflow Burner:* Same coaxial burner used in the ACME CLD Flame experiment, surrounding the fuel jet with a conditioned synthetic air coflow to evaluate lifted flame stability.
- **High-Voltage Electrode Mesh:**
  - A circular, fine-mesh copper electrode suspended downstream of the burner tip.

- A circular, fine-mesh copper electrode suspended downstream of the burner tip.

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Generation of Ion-Driven Convection in Microgravity:**
   - In microgravity, electric fields generated significant ion-driven convective velocities ($0.1 - 0.5\ \text{m/s}$) that altered the entire flow field around the flame.
   - Depending on electrode polarity, the ionic wind could either pull the flame toward the electrode mesh (elongating the flame) or push the flame back toward the burner rim (flattening the flame into a broad disc).
title: NASA PSI-22: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames)

text:
2. **Electrostatic Soot Suppression & Trajectory Control:**
   - Nascent soot particles acquire electrical charges in the flame zone.
   - Applying an electric field enabled direct electrostatic steering of soot particles. Guiding soot through high-temperature oxidizer zones accelerated soot burnout, **virtually eliminating soot emission and smoke-point breakthrough** in ethylene flames that were heavily sooting under zero-field conditions.

3. **Active Liftoff Stabilization & Blowoff Prevention:**
   - Electric field forces altered the local velocity strain at the flame base. By tuning field voltage, near-limit lifted flames that were on the verge of blowing out could be actively pulled back and stabilized at the burner rim.
title: NASA PSI-22: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames)

text:
4. **Voltage-Current ($I-V$) Characteristics & Model Validation (25 Archival Papers):**
   - Flight data mapped complete sub-saturation, saturation, and secondary ionization regimes for non-premixed flames in 0g.
   - Validated numerical plasma-combustion models developed by UC Irvine (Chien, Dunn-Rankin) and international collaborators, providing benchmark formulas for chemi-ion production rates.

## 2. Executive Summary & Spherical Diffusion Flame Physics Rationale
Diffusion flames represent the core reacting flow structure of combustion engines, furnaces, and accidental fires. In terrestrial 1g environments, buoyancy-driven natural convection ($Gr \gg 1$) distorts flames into asymmetric conical geometries, forcing multi-dimensional flow strains that obscure the coupling between fluid transport, thermal radiation, and chemical kinetics.
title: NASA PSI-23: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame)

text:
In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, buoyancy is eliminated ($Gr \to 0$). The **ACME Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame)** experiment established spherically symmetric, nominally one-dimensional diffusion flames by issuing gaseous fuel mixtures radially outward through a porous spherical burner into an oxidizing ambient atmosphere. This 1D spherical geometry provided the most mathematically rigorous and pristine experimental testbed possible to:
1. **Assess High-Order Chemistry & Radiation Models:** Provide 1D experimental benchmark data (temperature profiles, chemiluminescence distributions, and extinction limits) to test detailed chemical kinetics and radiation transfer models without multi-dimensional aerodynamic complications.
title: NASA PSI-23: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame)

text:
2. **Dual Flame Extinction Limits:** Determine both the **convective / chemical-kinetic extinction limit** (occurring at low Damköhler numbers, $Da$, where high flow rates induce strain-induced blowout) and the **radiative extinction limit** (occurring at high Damköhler numbers, $Da$, where long residence times allow radiant heat loss to cool the flame below critical reaction temperatures).
3. **Pulsating Flame Instabilities:** Empirically verify the theoretical prediction that transient spherical diffusion flames exhibit oscillatory pulsating instabilities when the fuel/diluent mixture exceeds a critical Lewis number ($Le > Le_c$).
title: NASA PSI-23: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame)

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Dual Extinction Boundaries (The U-Shaped Flammability Curve):**
   - ACME s-Flame mapped complete flammability boundaries across fuel flow rate and oxygen concentration, proving the existence of a continuous U-shaped extinction curve in Damköhler number ($Da$) space.
   - At high fuel flow rates, flames extinguished due to kinetic strain and residence-time limitation. At very low fuel flow rates, flames grew into wide, diffuse spherical shells that extinguished cleanly via radiative cooling, establishing the ultimate low-velocity extinction boundary.
title: NASA PSI-23: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame)

text:
2. **Observation of Pulsating Flame Front Instabilities:**
   - Experimentally confirmed the existence of pulsating cellular instabilities in spherical diffusion flames.
   - For fuel mixtures with Lewis numbers exceeding critical values ($Le > Le_c$, achieved by helium dilution), the flame front exhibited self-excited radial oscillations in diameter, temperature, and radical luminescence prior to extinction.

3. **Double Luminous Reaction Zone in H$_2$/CH$_4$ Blends:**
   - Observed a distinct double reaction zone structure in spherical $\text{H}_2/\text{CH}_4$ diffusion flames, where hydrogen oxidizes in an inner reaction front while methane-derived radicals react in a secondary outer zone, driven by mass diffusivity differences ($Le_{\text{H}_2} \ll Le_{\text{CH}_4}$).
title: NASA PSI-23: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame)

text:
4. **Benchmark Model Validation (44 Archival Papers):**
   - Provided benchmark 1D validation data for transient numerical simulations developed by Princeton, Rutgers, and NASA GRC. Numerical models coupling detailed transport, chemical kinetics, and spectral radiation matched measured flame radii, radical profiles, and extinction flow rates within $< 4\%$ error.

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Spacecraft Cabin Gaseous Fuel Leak Flammability:**
   - Pressurized hydrogen and methane lines are critical components of life support sabatier reactors, fuel cells, and propulsion modules.
   - ACME s-Flame proved that 1D spherical diffusion flames can sustain combustion at exceptionally low fuel supply rates where buoyant 1g flames blow out, meaning small hairline gas leaks in microgravity can create persistent, stable spherical flames.
title: NASA PSI-23: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame)

text:
2. **Radiative Extinction Limits for Fire Suppression:**
   - Quantified the precise radiation-loss Damköhler number required to induce radiative extinction. This defines the minimum dilution of carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) or nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$) required to extinguish gaseous fires in spacecraft habitats without relying on buoyant convective cooling.

3. **Combustion Sensor Thresholding:**
   - Documented the spectral chemiluminescence signatures ($\text{OH}^*$, $\text{CH}^*$) and radiant heat flux of near-extinction spherical flames, providing empirical calibration data for spacecraft optical flame detectors.

## 2. Executive Summary & Historical Discovery of Cool Flame Droplet Burning
The **Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)** represents a landmark investigation in the history of combustion science and microgravity research. Conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), FLEX was originally formulated to investigate the extinction behavior and flammability limits of isolated liquid hydrocarbon and alcohol droplets in quiescent microgravity environments, quantify the efficacy of gaseous fire suppressants ($\text{CO}_2$, $\text{He}$, $\text{SF}_6$), and validate multi-dimensional numerical combustion models.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
During flight operations between 2009 and 2011, FLEX produced one of the most unexpected and transformative scientific breakthroughs of the space program: the definitive experimental discovery of **quasi-steady cool flame droplet combustion**. 
- When large alkane droplets ($n$-heptane, $n$-octane, $n$-decane) were ignited in microgravity, their hot diffusion flames ($T \approx 1800 - 2000\ \text{K}$) burned until radiative heat loss from accumulated soot particles and combustion products cooled the flame, forcing visible hot-flame extinction at a finite droplet diameter.
- Instead of stopping evaporation, the fuel droplet surprisingly continued to shrink and vaporize at a steady, measurable rate without any visible flame emission or detectible soot luminescence.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text: - Intensive diagnostic analysis and asymptotic kinetic modeling revealed that a second-stage, low-temperature reaction zone ($T \approx 600 - 900\ \text{K}$) had formed around the droplet. Supported by low-temperature hydrocarbon oxidation kinetics (negative temperature coefficient alkylperoxy radical chemistry), these quasi-steady "cool flames" continued burning until a second, distinct low-temperature extinction diameter was reached.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
This discovery revolutionized combustion kinetics, transformed droplet burning theory, and uncovered major unpredicted fire hazards for human spaceflight missions.

---
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
## 3. Flight Architecture & The FLEX Experimental Apparatus
The FLEX investigation was deployed in the Destiny Laboratory module of the ISS using the **Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)** and the **Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)**:
- **Droplet Deployment & Support:**
  - *Fiber-Supported Droplets:* Droplets suspended on fine silicon-carbide (SiC) fibers ($d_{\text{fiber}} \approx 14\ \mu\text{m}$) with bead anchor points, allowing precise positioning at the optical focal center.
  - *Free-Floating Droplets:* Free droplets deployed without physical tethering via opposed dispensing needles with rapid retraction, eliminating conduction heat losses and fiber-induced flow distortion.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
- *Initial Droplet Diameters:* Systematically varied from $d_0 \approx 1.5\ \text{mm}$ to $5.0\ \text{mm}$.
- **Atmospheric Environment Control:**
  - Ambient pressures: Ranging from sub-atmospheric to elevated levels ($0.5\ \text{atm} \le P \le 1.5\ \text{atm}$).
  - Oxidizer compositions: Oxygen mole fractions varied from above ambient ($Y_{\text{O}_2} \approx 0.30$) down to the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI, $Y_{\text{O}_2} \approx 0.12 - 0.14$).
  - Gaseous suppressants and inerts: Carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$), helium ($\text{He}$), sulfur hexafluoride ($\text{SF}_6$), and nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$).
- **Test Procedures for Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI):**

- **Test Procedures for Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI):**
  - Iterative tests at fixed pressure and droplet size, progressively stepping down oxygen mole fraction until droplets either burn to completion, extinguish radiatively, or fail to ignite.
