## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data

1. **Discovery of Quasi-Steady Cool Flame Droplet Burning:**
   - FLEX established that low-temperature alkane oxidation chemistry can sustain quasi-steady diffusion flames around liquid droplets in the absence of buoyant convection.
   - For $n$-heptane, hot flame extinction occurred at diameters $d_{\text{ext,hot}} \approx 1.5 - 2.5\ \text{mm}$, followed immediately by an invisible cool flame burning period lasting several seconds with burning rate constants $K_{\text{cool}} \approx (0.3 - 0.5) K_{\text{hot}}$ ($K \equiv -d(d^2)/dt$), terminating at a final cool-flame extinction diameter $d_{\text{ext,cool}} \approx 0.5 - 0.9\ \text{mm}$.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
2. **Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) & Suppressant Effectiveness Ranking:**
   - The LOI was precisely mapped as a function of ambient pressure ($0.5 - 1.5\ \text{atm}$) and diluent species.
   - Suppressant efficacy per mole followed the sequence: $\text{SF}_6 \gg \text{CO}_2 > \text{He} > \text{N}_2$.
   - $\text{SF}_6$ demonstrated extraordinary suppression capability due to its exceptionally high molecular heat capacity, which rapidly cools flame temperatures below the kinetic threshold for chain branching.
   - $\text{He}$ promoted high thermal conductivity, increasing heat loss from the reaction zone but enhancing mass transport.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text: - $\text{CO}_2$ acted both through thermal heat capacity and direct chemical participation via the reverse water-gas shift reaction ($\text{CO}_2 + \text{H} \rightleftharpoons \text{CO} + \text{OH}$).
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
3. **Soot Shell Dynamics & Radiative Extinction Limits:**
   - Spherically symmetric microgravity combustion traps soot particles in an annular shell between the droplet surface and the flame sheet, driven by the balance between Stefan flow drag and outward thermophoretic forces.
   - For droplets with initial diameters $d_0 > 2.5\ \text{mm}$, intense radiative emission from this concentrated soot shell leads to severe radiant heat loss fractions ($\chi_{\text{rad}} > 0.35$), cooling the flame and causing premature radiative extinction before fuel depletion.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
4. **Convective Drift & Sub-Buoyant Flow Sensitivities:**
   - Experiments with drifting free droplets revealed that even minor relative velocities ($1 - 5\ \text{mm/s}$) rupture the spherical symmetry of the soot shell, creating an open wake that allows soot venting.
   - This convective ventilation reduces radiative heat loss, paradoxically extending hot-flame survival and altering extinction diameters compared to strictly quiescent conditions.

5. **Water Condensation and Dissolution in Methanol Combustion:**
   - Methanol droplet tests revealed substantial water vapor absorption from the combustion product shell into the liquid droplet core, continuously diluting the fuel and driving dynamic shifts in burning rates and extinction limits.

title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Hazard of Undetectable Cool Flame Fires:**
   - Cool flames emit virtually zero visible light and have negligible blackbody infrared radiation, making them completely undetectable by standard spacecraft optical flame detectors and crew human vision.
   - A localized liquid leak (e.g., thermal control fluid, lubricant, or propellant) ignited in microgravity could extinguish its hot flame, leading crew to believe the fire is out, while an invisible cool flame continues consuming cabin oxygen and generating toxic carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$).
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
2. **Catastrophic Flashover & Re-Ignition Hazards:**
   - FLEX demonstrated that surviving cool flames can abruptly transition back into roaring hot diffusion flames if cabin ventilation fans ramp up, oxygen concentration rises, or pressure changes occur.
   - Spacecraft fire emergency procedures must mandate prolonged inert gas flooding and active toxic gas scrubbing even after visible flames vanish.
title: NASA PSI-69: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX Droplet Combustion & Suppression)

text:
3. **Fire Suppression System Sizing & Extinguisher Design:**
   - Traditional terrestrial fire extinguishing standards (e.g., NFPA 12, NFPA 2001) rely on buoyantly dominated extinction criteria that severely underestimate the concentration of gaseous agent ($\text{CO}_2$ or $\text{N}_2$) required to suppress cool flames in microgravity.
   - FLEX data provide the foundational empirical baseline for NASA's spacecraft fire safety standards (NASA-STD-6001) and exploration atmosphere life support sizing (e.g., 8.2 psi / 34% $\text{O}_2$ exploration atmospheres for Artemis and Lunar Gateway).

## 2. Executive Summary & Solid Fuel Combustion Physics Rationale
The **Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)** flight investigation was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG). BASS was designed to address fundamental gaps in spacecraft fire safety, specifically the discrepancies between normal-gravity material flammability screening standards (such as NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), ground-based short-duration drop tower experiments, and actual steady-state solid fuel combustion in low-gravity space habitats.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
The core hypothesis of BASS is that solid materials in microgravity—when exposed to low-speed forced ventilation typical of spacecraft cabin environmental control systems ($1\ \text{cm/s} \le u_{\text{flow}} \le 20\ \text{cm/s}$)—burn as readily, and often *more vigorously* and across a *broader flammability envelope*, than identical materials tested under normal 1g gravity.
- In terrestrial 1g environments, buoyancy-induced natural convection generates rapid upward flow ($u_{\text{buoy}} \approx 20 - 30\ \text{cm/s}$) that sweeps heat away from thin fuel surfaces and imposes aerodynamic strain on flame stabilization bases.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
- In microgravity, buoyancy is eliminated ($Gr \to 0$), enabling low forced flow velocities where residence times are long, convective cooling is minimized, and conductive/radiative heat feedback from the flame to the pyrolyzing solid fuel is maximized.
- BASS provided extended microgravity burn times (several minutes per test) that were impossible to attain in 2.2-second or 5.18-second terrestrial drop towers, allowing solid fuels with finite thermal thickness to reach steady-state thermal penetration, pyrolysis, and flame spread.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)
NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

## 3. Flight Architecture & The BASS Experimental Apparatus
The BASS payload was installed within the sealed, negative-pressure working volume of the **Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)** on the ISS:
- **Flow Tunnel & Flow Conditioning:**
  - A compact clear polycarbonate flow duct with a square internal cross section measuring $76\ \text{mm} \times 76\ \text{mm}$ ($3\ \text{in} \times 3\ \text{in}$) and a length of approximately $350\ \text{mm}$.
  - Variable-speed DC ventilation fan capable of producing steady, conditioned forced airflows across fuel surfaces spanning from $0.5\ \text{cm/s}$ to $40\ \text{cm/s}$.
  - Flow configurations supported both:
    1. *Opposed-flow:* Forced airflow directed against the direction of flame front propagation.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
1. *Opposed-flow:* Forced airflow directed against the direction of flame front propagation.
    2. *Concurrent-flow:* Forced airflow directed in the same direction as flame front spread.
- **Ignition System:**
  - Precision 29-gage Kanthal resistance heating wire woven across one edge of the fuel sample, powered by controlled DC pulse discharges to ensure repeatable ignition without excessive charring.
- **Solid Fuel Types & Geometries:**
  - *Cotton/Fiberglass Blended Fabric:* Custom-woven thin fabric composed of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass by mass. The inert fiberglass matrix provided structural integrity, preventing the pyrolyzing fabric from curling, flapping, or disintegrating under airflow, thus maintaining a rigid two-dimensional geometry throughout the burn.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
- *Engineering Polymers:* Flat sheets and strips of Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), flame-resistant meta-aramid Nomex fabric, and polyetherimide (Ultem).
  - *Geometrical Variations:* Flat sheet samples, cylindrical rods, solid spheres, and wake-flow configurations where fuel samples were placed immediately downstream of flow obstructions to simulate fires behind equipment racks.
- **Extinguishment & Suppression Hardware:**
  - Gaseous nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$) injection system calibrated to introduce inert gas into the flow stream at controlled flow rates, testing gaseous fire extinguishment limits and evaluating the dynamic suppression response of solid fuel flames.

## 4. Key Scientific Discoveries & Technical Data
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
1. **Enhanced Flammability and U-Shaped Extinction Boundaries:**
   - BASS conclusively confirmed that the flammability corridor for solid fuels in microgravity is bounded by a characteristic U-shaped extinction curve plotted against forced flow velocity:
     - *Radiative Extinction Limit:* At very low flow velocities ($u < 1 - 2\ \text{cm/s}$), flame spread rates plummet and flames extinguish due to excessive radiant heat loss from carbon dioxide, water vapor, and soot without sufficient convective replenishment of oxygen.
     - *Convective Blowout Limit:* At high velocities ($u > 30 - 40\ \text{cm/s}$), aerodynamic strain exceeds the chemical reaction rate, pushing the reaction zone downstream and extinguishing the flame base.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text: - *Peak Flame Spread Regime:* Maximum flame spread rates occurred at intermediate flow speeds ($u \approx 5 - 15\ \text{cm/s}$), an airflow range directly corresponding to standard cabin ventilation velocities aboard crewed spacecraft.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
2. **Inadequacy of NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 for Low-Gravity Screening:**
   - Materials that easily passed normal-gravity vertical upward flammability screening (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) by self-extinguishing in 1g were observed to ignite, sustain stable flames, and spread completely across the sample in microgravity when subjected to low-speed forced flows ($u \approx 2 - 10\ \text{cm/s}$).
   - This showed that 1g testing is non-conservative for thin materials and fabrics due to buoyancy-induced cooling and flame stretching.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
3. **Effective Velocity Correlation ($u_{\text{eff}}$) & Boundary Layer Effects:**
   - Established that duct wall and fuel surface aerodynamic boundary layer development alters the local flow speed experienced by the flame.
   - BASS researchers developed an empirical-theoretical effective velocity correlation:
     $$u_{\text{eff}} = u_{\infty} f(\delta / L_{\text{flame}})$$
     that successfully collapsed microgravity opposed-flow flame spread rates across diverse sample widths and duct positions onto a universal thermal-regime scaling curve.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
4. **Wake Flame Stability Behind Obstacles:**
   - Fuel samples positioned behind aerodynamic flow obstructions exhibited robust wake flames. The recirculation vortex behind the bluff body trapped heat and reactive species while shielding the flame base from high-speed crossflows, allowing flames to persist at overall duct airspeeds that would cause blowoff on unobstructed flat fuels.
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
5. **Gaseous Nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$) Suppression Thresholds:**
   - Quantified the critical nitrogen concentration required to extinguish spreading solid flames under varied forced convective velocities.
   - At low flow speeds near the radiative boundary, small increases in nitrogen concentration rapidly quenched the flame, whereas at intermediate speeds ($u \approx 10\ \text{cm/s}$), higher nitrogen concentrations were required due to optimal stoichiometric mixing.

## 5. Spacecraft Fire Safety Engineering & Life Support Ramifications

1. **Spacecraft Ventilation Protocols During Fire Emergencies:**
   - Previous emergency procedures often recommended reducing cabin ventilation to minimal levels to "starve" a fire. BASS flight data proved this strategy is dangerous: reducing airflow from nominal speeds ($15\ \text{cm/s}$) down to $5\ \text{cm/s}$ moves the solid fuel directly into its peak flammability and fastest spread regime.
   - Modern spacecraft protocols mandate complete and immediate shutdown of all environmental circulation fans (rapid isolation) to force the fire into the oxygen-starved radiative extinction regime ($u \to 0$).
title: NASA PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS Solid Fuel Microgravity Investigation)

text:
2. **Fire Suppression System Design & Inerting Requirements:**
   - BASS data provided baseline extinction limits for sizing total-flooding nitrogen and carbon dioxide fire suppression systems for the ISS, the Orion Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle (MPCV), and the Lunar Gateway.
   - Suppression agent discharge must be designed to avoid inducing turbulent mixing jets that temporarily supply oxygen and ventilate fuel surfaces.

3. **Performance-Based Material Qualification:**
   - The findings of BASS laid the scientific groundwork for modernizing NASA-STD-6001 by introducing low-pressure, oxygen-enriched, and microgravity flammability characterization tools, bridging empirical ground tests with computational fire propagation codes.
